principles.name: Hick's Law
principles.summary: Decision time increases as the number and complexity of choices increase.
principles.description: Reduce unnecessary options, organize decisions clearly, and guide users toward the most likely next action to speed up task completion.
principles.whenToUse: Use in approvals, menus, settings, dashboards, and task flows where users must choose among multiple actions.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle is strongest when users face many competing actions or unclear decision paths.

actions.title: Reduce choice options
actions.description: Limit dropdown menus to 5-7 items max; use progressive disclosure for advanced options.

actions.title: Create visual hierarchy
actions.description: Use size, color, and spacing to guide attention to primary vs. secondary actions.

actions.title: Group related choices
actions.description: Organize options into logical categories to reduce scanning time.

antiPatterns: Long dropdown menus with too many options
Presenting primary and secondary actions with equal visual weight
Nested decision trees without clear defaults
uiPatterns: Segmented controls for primary actions
Progressive disclosure for advanced settings
Grouped action menus with recommended defaults
examples: Approval flow that surfaces approve, reject, and request changes before showing secondary actions.
Checkout screen that highlights one recommended shipping option instead of many equal choices.
principles.designPrompt: Identify the top 3 actions per screen. Demote everything else to secondary or overflow.

principles.name: Miller's Law
principles.summary: People can hold only a limited amount of information in working memory at once.
principles.description: Chunk information into smaller groups and reveal complexity gradually to help users process and recall what matters.
principles.whenToUse: Use in complex forms, dashboards, setup flows, and dense content experiences.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle is critical when users must remember instructions, compare multiple data points, or process dense forms.

actions.title: Chunk information
actions.description: Group related items into 5-9 item clusters with clear visual separation.

actions.title: Use progressive disclosure
actions.description: Show primary information first and reveal secondary details on demand.

actions.title: Provide memory aids
actions.description: Add tooltips, helper text, summaries, and inline validation to reduce memory burden.

antiPatterns: Forms with too many visible fields at once
Large tables without grouping or hierarchy
Instructions that disappear before task completion
uiPatterns: Step-by-step wizards
Accordion sections for related content
Sticky summaries during multi-step completion
examples: Enterprise form grouped into contact, billing, permissions, and review sections.
Admin dashboard where metrics are chunked by category instead of one flat grid.
principles.designPrompt: Count every item in every menu. More than 7? Group or collapse. No exceptions.

principles.name: Von Restorff Effect
principles.summary: Items that differ from their surroundings are more likely to be noticed and remembered.
principles.description: Use contrast selectively to call attention to critical actions, warnings, and key states without overwhelming the interface.
principles.whenToUse: Use for alerts, dangerous actions, critical tasks, and any place where users must notice one thing quickly.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle matters most when important signals risk being lost inside repetitive or visually dense interfaces.

actions.title: Highlight key elements
actions.description: Use color, size, or position to make critical actions and information stand out.

actions.title: Create visual contrast
actions.description: Make primary CTA buttons distinctly different from secondary actions.

actions.title: Isolate warnings
actions.description: Present error messages and alerts in visually distinct containers.

antiPatterns: Too many competing highlight colors
Making every banner urgent
Critical and routine states sharing the same visual style
uiPatterns: Priority badges in tables
Distinct destructive action styling
Escalated alert cards with icon and contrast
examples: Operational dashboard where critical incidents use a unique visual treatment distinct from informational logs.
Confirmation modal where the destructive option is clearly differentiated.
principles.designPrompt: Reserve your highest visual contrast for one element per screen only. Everything else stays neutral.

principles.name: Fitts's Law
principles.summary: The time to acquire a target depends on its size and distance.
principles.description: Make important controls larger, closer, and easier to reach so users can act accurately and quickly.
principles.whenToUse: Use in forms, mobile controls, navigation, and any interaction with repeated clicking or tapping.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle is especially useful when users struggle with precision, speed, or repeated input actions.

actions.title: Increase target size
actions.description: Make touch targets at least 44x44px for easy tapping.

actions.title: Reduce distance
actions.description: Place related actions close together and near the current task focus.

actions.title: Use reachable placement
actions.description: Anchor primary mobile actions within thumb-friendly zones.

antiPatterns: Tiny tap targets
Primary actions isolated far from the task
Dense clusters of interactive controls
uiPatterns: Sticky submit bars
Floating action buttons
Bottom action areas on mobile
examples: Form submit button anchored near the final field instead of buried in distant page chrome.
Mobile menu items with adequate touch spacing for gloved or rushed use.
principles.designPrompt: Make the primary action the largest and most central button on any key screen.

principles.name: Serial Position Effect
principles.summary: Users remember the first and last items in a sequence better than the middle items.
principles.description: Place the most important options at the beginning or end of lists, menus, and step sequences.
principles.whenToUse: Use in navigation, approval lists, stepper flows, and long option lists.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle helps when important actions are being missed because of their position in a list or menu.

actions.title: Prioritize top and bottom positions
actions.description: Place the most important items first and last in menus and ordered groups.

actions.title: Use recency for final actions
actions.description: Position confirmations or next-step calls to action near the end of flows.

actions.title: Break up long lists
actions.description: Reduce middle-item drop-off by splitting long lists into groups.

antiPatterns: Burying key tasks in the middle of long lists
Equal treatment for all menu items regardless of importance
Long flat navigation without grouping
uiPatterns: Pinned first/last menu items
Grouped navigation sections
Top summary and bottom completion actions
examples: Priority filters surfaced first in a reporting menu while export actions remain last.
Critical exit/save actions placed where users expect closure.
principles.designPrompt: Critical items go first or last in any list. Never bury them in the middle.

principles.name: Jakob's Law
principles.summary: Users prefer interfaces that behave like the ones they already know.
principles.description: Follow established UI conventions to reduce friction, confusion, and learning time.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding, navigation, forms, dashboards, and any workflow intended for quick adoption.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle is valuable when users need speed, confidence, and low training overhead.

actions.title: Use standard patterns
actions.description: Follow established UI conventions for search, navigation, forms, and feedback.

actions.title: Maintain consistency
actions.description: Keep patterns and terminology consistent across the product.

actions.title: Match mental models
actions.description: Design workflows around user expectations rather than internal system structure.

antiPatterns: Inventing unfamiliar control patterns without a strong reason
Changing common icon meanings
Using inconsistent terminology across screens
uiPatterns: Conventional top navigation and breadcrumbs
Standard filter/search layouts
Recognizable settings and profile patterns
examples: Using a familiar left-nav + content pane structure in enterprise software.
Applying standard search placement and filtering patterns in data-heavy tools.
principles.designPrompt: Audit complex components: do they match conventions from the top 3 tools your users already know?

principles.name: Peak-End Rule
principles.summary: People judge an experience largely by its most intense moment and its ending.
principles.description: Design meaningful peaks and strong endings so users leave workflows with confidence and clarity.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding, submissions, approvals, setup completion, and handoff workflows.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle matters when completion quality and perceived confidence are key outcomes.

actions.title: Design for meaningful moments
actions.description: Create positive peaks at decisive or rewarding moments.

actions.title: End with clarity
actions.description: Use strong completion states with clear next steps and confirmation.

actions.title: Reduce negative peaks
actions.description: Avoid abrupt failures or unclear endings in critical workflows.

antiPatterns: Generic completion states
Abrupt task endings with no next-step guidance
High-friction confirmations at the end of long flows
uiPatterns: Rich success screens
Completion summaries
Celebratory but restrained progress milestones
examples: Submission confirmation that explains what happens next and who owns the task.
Project handoff flow ending with a concise summary and teammate notification.
principles.designPrompt: Design the last screen of every task flow as carefully as the first.

principles.name: Progressive Disclosure
principles.summary: Reveal only the information and controls users need at the current moment.
principles.description: Reduce overwhelm by presenting core tasks first and exposing additional complexity only when needed.
principles.whenToUse: Use in forms, advanced settings, admin tools, and expert workflows with optional complexity.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle is strongest when the interface has expert depth but should still feel simple at first glance.

actions.title: Start simple
actions.description: Show core functionality first and tuck advanced options behind disclosure patterns.

actions.title: Use smart defaults
actions.description: Preselect the most common or safe option to reduce decision effort.

actions.title: Reveal conditionally
actions.description: Show additional inputs only when previous selections require them.

antiPatterns: Showing every option by default
Mixing advanced settings with primary actions
Long forms without progressive grouping
uiPatterns: Accordions for advanced options
Conditional form sections
Collapsed detail rows with summary first
examples: Form that only shows dependent fields after a user selects a non-default path.
Analytics tool with advanced filters hidden until requested.
principles.designPrompt: Design every screen at two levels: basic (immediate) and advanced (discoverable).

principles.name: Doherty Threshold
principles.summary: Productivity rises when system response is fast enough that users do not have to wait.
principles.description: Fast response and clear feedback keep users in flow and reduce hesitation, especially in repeated operational tasks.
principles.whenToUse: Use wherever users submit, search, filter, validate, monitor, or repeatedly interact with the system.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle matters when speed, confidence, and continuity are essential to completing work.

actions.title: Optimize feedback speed
actions.description: Aim for immediate UI acknowledgement on input, filtering, and submission.

actions.title: Provide loading feedback
actions.description: Use skeletons, progress states, or optimistic updates when operations take longer.

actions.title: Reduce blocking waits
actions.description: Preload likely data and keep users moving while background work finishes.

antiPatterns: No visible response after a click
Full-screen loading for small updates
Blocking users from continuing without explanation
uiPatterns: Optimistic updates
Inline validation
Skeleton loaders for list refreshes
examples: Filter results updating instantly while preserving scroll context.
Form save that acknowledges success immediately and syncs in the background.
principles.designPrompt: Define a 400ms SLA for every user-triggered action. Show a skeleton loader for anything slower.

principles.name: Social Proof
principles.summary: People look to others' behavior for cues about what is safe, useful, or correct.
principles.description: Show relevant evidence of peer use, team adoption, or trusted validation to help users feel more confident in uncertain decisions.
principles.whenToUse: Use in collaborative workflows, handoff moments, high-uncertainty choices, and trust-sensitive experiences.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle matters when users need reassurance, confidence, or alignment with peers and stakeholders.

actions.title: Show relevant proof
actions.description: Display reviews, prior approvals, or teammate activity where it reduces uncertainty.

actions.title: Highlight trusted signals
actions.description: Use badges, audit history, and team endorsements to reinforce confidence.

actions.title: Make collaboration visible
actions.description: Show who acted, who reviewed, and what peers typically choose.

antiPatterns: Irrelevant or fake trust signals
No social context in shared workflows
Hiding activity history when it would increase confidence
uiPatterns: Reviewer activity panels
Usage or adoption badges
Inline audit history and collaborator presence
examples: Approval screen showing similar past decisions and peer reviewer comments.
Shared workspace that surfaces who completed, reviewed, or approved a task.
principles.designPrompt: Surface aggregate usage data wherever users face unfamiliar decisions.

principles.name: Cognitive Load Theory
principles.summary: Task performance degrades when interface demands exceed working memory capacity.
principles.description: Every UI element imposes either necessary task complexity or unnecessary interface friction. Reduce extraneous load — caused by poor layout, redundant steps, and split information — without stripping domain meaning.
principles.whenToUse: Use as the core diagnostic framework whenever users make errors, slow down, or abandon tasks that should be within their competence.
principles.whyItMatches: This is the root cause behind most cognitive overload failures and the framework that distinguishes what to remove from what must stay.

actions.title: Eliminate extraneous steps
actions.description: Remove navigation and input steps that add no task value.

actions.title: Co-locate dependent information
actions.description: Keep data needed to make a decision visible while the decision is being made.

actions.title: Reduce redundant representation
actions.description: Avoid presenting the same information twice unless each form serves a distinct purpose.

antiPatterns: Forcing users to remember values from a previous screen
Cluttering forms with help text that repeats the label
Splitting related fields across different pages or panels
uiPatterns: Inline summaries that persist while users complete dependent fields
Progressive disclosure to hide complexity until needed
Worked examples and templates for complex input tasks
examples: Medication ordering screen keeping patient weight, allergies, and dose constraints visible while the clinician selects the drug.
Multi-step form showing a persistent summary of prior answers while the user completes later sections.
principles.designPrompt: For every design element, ask: does this reduce task load or add to it?

principles.name: Inattentional Blindness
principles.summary: Users often fail to notice critical information when their attention is focused elsewhere.
principles.description: Even prominent UI elements go unseen if they fall outside the user's current attentional focus. The fix is not making things bigger — it is placing critical cues in the direct path of the primary task gaze.
principles.whenToUse: Use when important information is being missed despite being visually present, or when designing warning systems in task-dense interfaces.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle explains why 'the warning was right there' is not a defence — attentional blindness is a feature of normal cognition.

actions.title: Place critical cues on the task path
actions.description: Position warnings and errors directly adjacent to the action they affect.

actions.title: Use just-in-time prompts
actions.description: Surface critical information at the moment of decision, not before or after.

actions.title: Reserve acknowledgement for high-risk only
actions.description: Only require explicit acknowledgement for genuinely critical states.

antiPatterns: Global notification bars for errors that apply to a specific field
Persistent banners users learn to ignore through repetition
Warnings positioned above the fold while the action is below
uiPatterns: Inline error messages beside the failing field
Contextual tooltips triggered at the moment of interaction
Interstitial confirmation only for irreversible high-risk actions
examples: Critical lab value displayed inline in the order row it affects, not only in a global notification tray.
Payment error surfaced beside the failing card field, not in a toast at the top of the page.
principles.designPrompt: Place critical information in the direct path of the user's primary task gaze.

principles.name: Change Blindness
principles.summary: Users often fail to notice changes in a display unless the change is explicitly signalled.
principles.description: When information updates without a clear visual transient, users build mental models from the old state. In collaboration and monitoring contexts, this leads to decisions made on stale data.
principles.whenToUse: Use when data updates asynchronously, when multiple users edit shared records, or when status can change between views.
principles.whyItMatches: Silent updates in dashboards and shared records are a primary source of errors from this effect.

actions.title: Highlight changed fields
actions.description: Use colour, motion, or badges to mark fields that changed since the user last viewed them.

actions.title: Show last-updated timestamps
actions.description: Display when values were last changed and by whom so users can assess data freshness.

actions.title: Provide diff views for editable records
actions.description: In collaborative editing contexts, show what changed between versions.

antiPatterns: Quietly overwriting values without a visible indicator
Refreshing data tables without a change signal
Shared records with no audit trail or change history
uiPatterns: Row-level change indicators with timestamps
Animated highlight fading after update
Version diff panels in collaborative documents
examples: Medication reconciliation screen highlighting dose changes since the last visit in amber.
Shared spreadsheet that flashes updated cells with the editor's name on hover.
principles.designPrompt: Any data that changes asynchronously must have a visible change indicator.

principles.name: Attentional Blink
principles.summary: After detecting one event, users have a brief window during which they miss a second event.
principles.description: When two critical signals appear within ~500ms of each other, the second is frequently missed. Alert systems that stack notifications in rapid succession cause the second event to go unnoticed.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing alert and notification systems, especially in monitoring, clinical, or operational dashboards.
principles.whyItMatches: Alarm fatigue in high-stakes environments is frequently caused by this temporal processing limit, not user inattention.

actions.title: Rate-limit alert delivery
actions.description: Space critical notifications so users can process and respond to each before the next appears.

actions.title: Group concurrent alerts
actions.description: Consolidate simultaneous notifications into a single prioritised summary.

actions.title: Persist unacknowledged critical alerts
actions.description: Ensure high-severity alerts remain visible until acknowledged, rather than auto-dismissing.

antiPatterns: Toast notifications that stack and auto-dismiss
Firing multiple modal alerts in rapid succession
Treating all alerts as equally urgent regardless of severity
uiPatterns: Tiered alert inbox with priority ordering
Grouped notification summaries with expand-to-detail
Persistent critical alert banners requiring explicit dismissal
examples: ICU monitoring system consolidating concurrent alarms into a prioritised panel rather than overlapping modals.
Security system that queues alerts one at a time with a minimum 2-second gap between them.
principles.designPrompt: Never stack critical alerts. One at a time with clear dismissal before the next appears.

principles.name: Stroop Effect
principles.summary: When visual presentation conflicts with meaning, processing slows and errors increase.
principles.description: A green button labelled 'Delete' or a red badge meaning 'healthy' forces users to override automatic interpretation, consuming attentional resources and increasing errors.
principles.whenToUse: Use when auditing colour use, iconography, and label conventions — especially for status indicators and action buttons.
principles.whyItMatches: Semantic/visual mismatches cause real errors, not just aesthetic complaints.

actions.title: Align colour with universal semantics
actions.description: Use red exclusively for danger or error, green for safe or success — never swap these conventions.

actions.title: Make icon meaning consistent
actions.description: Ensure the same icon carries the same meaning across every screen in the product.

actions.title: Audit status indicator mappings
actions.description: Review every status badge, alert colour, and label combination for semantic alignment.

antiPatterns: Red used for normal-range values in clinical data tables
Same icon used for both archive and delete actions
Green confirm button on a destructive action modal
uiPatterns: Strict design-token colour-to-meaning map applied globally
Icon + label pairs that reinforce rather than contradict each other
Status system with distinct visual signatures per severity level
examples: Clinical results table reserving red highlighting for genuinely abnormal values only.
Destructive action confirmation using amber or red, never the default primary colour.
principles.designPrompt: Audit every status indicator: does visual style match semantic meaning? Red = danger, always.

principles.name: Recognition over Recall
principles.summary: Recognising an option from a list is far less cognitively demanding than retrieving it from memory.
principles.description: Every free-text field that has a finite valid set of answers is a recall demand. Replacing it with a searchable dropdown or autocomplete converts that demand to recognition, dramatically reducing errors.
principles.whenToUse: Use whenever inputs have a bounded valid set: country, status, user, product, or any controlled vocabulary.
principles.whyItMatches: Free-text fields for finite-value inputs are among the most common sources of input error in enterprise tools.

actions.title: Replace free text with searchable selections
actions.description: Convert any input with a known finite set of valid values to a dropdown, autocomplete, or picker.

actions.title: Surface recently used items
actions.description: Show recently or frequently used options at the top of lists for one-tap selection.

actions.title: Use inline type-ahead
actions.description: Filter options dynamically as the user types so they never need to know the exact value.

antiPatterns: Free-text fields for values like country, status, or category
Long dropdowns with no search capability
Requiring users to type exact codes or identifiers from memory
uiPatterns: Searchable select with type-ahead filtering
Command palette for navigating to actions and records
Recently used panel at the top of all search results
examples: Patient lookup field that filters by name, ID, or date of birth as the user types.
Permission assignment picker showing role names with descriptions rather than requiring code entry.
principles.designPrompt: Replace every free-text input that has finite valid values with a selection component.

principles.name: Zeigarnik Effect
principles.summary: Incomplete tasks occupy working memory until they are finished or explicitly set aside.
principles.description: Interrupted workflows leave an open loop in working memory that competes with other tasks. Saving progress and surfacing resume cues reduce this ambient cognitive drain.
principles.whenToUse: Use in multi-step flows, long forms, and collaborative tasks where interruptions are likely.
principles.whyItMatches: This explains why users who abandon a flow mid-way are harder to re-engage and why unfinished tasks feel distracting.

actions.title: Autosave and resume
actions.description: Save progress automatically and surface a clear 'continue where you left off' entry point.

actions.title: Surface incomplete tasks
actions.description: Show open tasks prominently so users can consciously defer rather than passively forget.

actions.title: Provide explicit closure
actions.description: Design completion states that clearly signal a task is done so the mental loop can close.

antiPatterns: Multi-step forms that lose progress on navigation or timeout
No indication of incomplete or partially submitted tasks
Completion states that feel ambiguous or anti-climactic
uiPatterns: Draft indicator with last-saved timestamp
Resume card on dashboard surfacing in-progress tasks
Explicit completion confirmation screen
examples: Procurement form persisting draft state across sessions with a 'Resume' CTA on the home screen.
Onboarding checklist that marks completed steps and persists incomplete items until closed.
principles.designPrompt: Persist and surface incomplete tasks. Closure reduces cognitive residue.

principles.name: Satisficing
principles.summary: Users stop searching and choose the first option that is good enough, not the optimal one.
principles.description: Users take the first path that meets a minimum threshold rather than evaluating all options. If the first visible path is also the safest and most appropriate one, satisficing works in everyone's favour.
principles.whenToUse: Use when the order and prominence of options have safety or quality implications.
principles.whyItMatches: Satisficing is a fundamental property of decision-making under cognitive constraint — designing against it causes preventable errors.

actions.title: Make the first option the right option
actions.description: Order defaults and suggestions so the most appropriate choice is the first one encountered.

actions.title: Use safe defaults
actions.description: Preselect the option correct for most users so satisficing leads to the right outcome.

actions.title: Reduce path length to the correct choice
actions.description: Minimise clicks between a user's goal and the best option for achieving it.

antiPatterns: Alphabetical ordering of options when importance ordering is possible
Dangerous or irreversible defaults in settings
Burying the safest option behind the most prominent one
uiPatterns: Recommended or default options visually distinguished
Search results ordered by relevance not recency
Pre-checked safe option with opt-out rather than opt-in
examples: Antibiotic selection dropdown listing first-line treatments first, not alphabetically.
Settings panel where the safest privacy option is pre-selected and changing requires deliberate action.
principles.designPrompt: Assume users take the first option they see. Make the first path the correct path.

principles.name: Confirmation Bias
principles.summary: People seek, interpret, and remember information that confirms their existing beliefs.
principles.description: Users rationalise confusing UX rather than flagging it, and interpret ambiguous interface states as confirming what they expected to happen. Design must present disconfirming signals clearly and use task-based testing rather than self-report.
principles.whenToUse: Use in testing methodology design, error message strategy, and any flow where users must evaluate conflicting information.
principles.whyItMatches: This explains why asking users 'was that easy?' is unreliable, and why users miss warning signs that contradict their expectation.

actions.title: Use task-based usability testing
actions.description: Observe behaviour rather than asking users to rate ease — people rationalise their experience after the fact.

actions.title: Design disconfirming signals to be unmissable
actions.description: Errors, warnings, and unexpected states must break through expectation, not blend into it.

actions.title: Provide explicit risk summaries
actions.description: In decision flows, surface the risks and downsides of the chosen option, not only the benefits.

antiPatterns: Post-task ease ratings as the primary usability metric
Warnings that look like standard UI components users learn to ignore
Decision summaries that only highlight benefits
uiPatterns: Task-completion metrics as research instrumentation
Distinct visual treatment for error and warning states
Risk/benefit balance panels in high-stakes choice flows
examples: Consent form presenting benefits and side effects with equivalent visual weight.
Usability test measuring time-on-task and error count rather than subjective ease scores.
principles.designPrompt: Never ask users "did you find that easy?" Watch behaviour — don't ask.

principles.name: Cognitive Ease
principles.summary: Easy-to-process information feels more familiar, trustworthy, and correct.
principles.description: Low-contrast text, jargon, and dense layouts create cognitive strain users unconsciously interpret as complexity or unreliability. Reducing this friction increases perceived trustworthiness and comprehension, not just aesthetic appeal.
principles.whenToUse: Use across all user-facing copy and layouts, with particular urgency in consent flows, onboarding, and error messages.
principles.whyItMatches: Cognitive ease explains why plain language improvements increase trust as well as comprehension.

actions.title: Use plain language
actions.description: Write at the reading level of your median user; remove jargon, passive voice, and nominalisations.

actions.title: Increase contrast and spacing
actions.description: Maintain a minimum 4.5:1 contrast ratio and generous line-height for body text.

actions.title: Use familiar visual conventions
actions.description: Match interface patterns to tools your users already know — novelty adds cognitive cost.

antiPatterns: Technical terminology in labels aimed at non-expert users
Dense, low-contrast instructional text
Novel interaction patterns without clear affordance cues
uiPatterns: Plain-language microcopy guidelines applied to all strings
Consistent visual system matching user mental models
High-contrast type at comfortable reading sizes
examples: Consent document rewritten at a Grade 8 reading level, increasing comprehension and completion rate.
Error message reading 'Your session expired. Please log in again.' instead of 'Authentication token invalid (403)'.
principles.designPrompt: Run every user-facing string through a plain-language check. Jargon equals distrust.

principles.name: Spacing Effect
principles.summary: Information learned across spaced intervals is retained far better than information massed into one session.
principles.description: Onboarding flows that introduce all features in a single tutorial waste most of that instruction — users retain only a fraction. Distributing feature discovery across first-use sessions and contextual in-app guidance dramatically improves long-term retention.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding, feature introduction, compliance training, and any scenario where users must retain procedural knowledge.
principles.whyItMatches: Most enterprise onboarding fails because it is designed for immediate completeness rather than long-term retention.

actions.title: Distribute feature discovery over time
actions.description: Introduce features progressively across the first several sessions rather than all at once.

actions.title: Use contextual nudges at point of use
actions.description: Surface tips when the user is about to perform a task for the first time, not during setup.

actions.title: Avoid single-session training for complex workflows
actions.description: Break complex procedural training into short, spaced modules with practical exercises.

antiPatterns: 30-minute onboarding tours that cover every feature before first use
All-or-nothing tutorial completion before the product unlocks
No contextual guidance after initial setup
uiPatterns: Progressive feature unlocking with contextual tips
In-product learning moments triggered by first use of a feature
Spaced reminder nudges for infrequently used features
examples: Enterprise tool introducing advanced reporting features only after a user has completed basic tasks three times.
Compliance platform sending weekly micro-lessons tied to the user's current workflow stage.
principles.designPrompt: Design feature discovery that unfolds over the first week of use, not a single tutorial.

principles.name: Dual Coding Theory
principles.summary: The brain processes verbal and visual information through separate channels; pairing both improves retention.
principles.description: When icons are paired with labels, or diagrams with explanations, the complementary channels reinforce each other in memory. The key is complementing — not duplicating — the same message across both channels.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing navigation, status indicators, and instructional content where comprehension and recall matter.
principles.whyItMatches: Icon-only navigation and diagram-only instructions both underuse this principle; pairing channels costs little and improves comprehension significantly.

actions.title: Pair icons with labels
actions.description: Always accompany icons with text labels in core navigation and action areas.

actions.title: Complement diagrams with explanations
actions.description: Place brief verbal descriptions alongside visual workflows so both channels reinforce the same message.

actions.title: Avoid redundant duplication
actions.description: Do not repeat the exact same content in both channels — each should add something the other cannot.

antiPatterns: Icon-only navigation for complex enterprise workflows
Diagrams with no accompanying text explanation
Text that simply narrates what is already fully visible in the image
uiPatterns: Icon + label navigation tabs
Status badges with both colour and text label
Annotated workflow diagrams
examples: Navigation bar showing both a home icon and the label 'Dashboard' for every primary destination.
Onboarding diagram pairing each step icon with a one-sentence action description.
principles.designPrompt: Never use icons without labels in enterprise tools. Pair every symbol with words.

principles.name: Law of Proximity
principles.summary: Elements placed close together are perceived as belonging to the same group.
principles.description: Spacing is the primary tool for communicating grouping — not borders or labels. Fields, labels, and actions that belong together must be close; those that are distinct must be spaced apart. Incorrect proximity creates wrong mental models of form structure.
principles.whenToUse: Use in every form layout, navigation structure, and information panel. Proximity misuse is one of the most common silent causes of user errors.
principles.whyItMatches: Proximity violations are often invisible to designers who know the intended grouping, but cause immediate confusion in testing.

actions.title: Use spacing as the primary grouping tool
actions.description: Increase gaps between groups and decrease gaps within groups before adding borders or backgrounds.

actions.title: Co-locate label and input
actions.description: Place form labels immediately above or beside their inputs with minimal gap.

actions.title: Audit spacing systematically
actions.description: Review every form and panel for cases where related items are further apart than unrelated ones.

antiPatterns: Form labels equally spaced from both the field above and the field below
Action buttons closer to the wrong section
Related metadata scattered across different parts of a card
uiPatterns: 8pt grid system with consistent spacing multiples
Field group containers with tighter internal than group-to-group spacing
Related action buttons grouped with the content they act on
examples: Form section where each label is 4px above its input and 20px below the previous input, making grouping clear.
Data card where primary metric, trend, and annotation are tightly grouped, separated from the action by larger space.
principles.designPrompt: Use spacing as your primary grouping tool. Close = related. Far = separate.

principles.name: Law of Similarity
principles.summary: Items that look alike are perceived as belonging to the same category or function.
principles.description: Visual similarity — colour, shape, size, weight — communicates membership. When read-only and editable fields look identical, or primary and secondary actions share the same visual weight, users misread the interface.
principles.whenToUse: Use when defining the visual language for interactive states, field types, action hierarchies, and status indicators.
principles.whyItMatches: Similarity violations cause confusion users experience as wrong actions or missed affordances, rarely tracing it back to visual inconsistency.

actions.title: Define a strict visual role system
actions.description: Assign one consistent visual pattern per interaction role: editable, read-only, and display values must each look distinct.

actions.title: Align visual weight with action importance
actions.description: Primary actions must look distinctly more prominent than secondary ones.

actions.title: Use consistent status colours
actions.description: Each status level must have a unique, consistent visual signature throughout the product.

antiPatterns: Editable and read-only fields using identical styling
Primary and secondary buttons with the same visual weight
Two different statuses rendered with the same colour in different parts of the product
uiPatterns: Design token system with distinct role-based component styles
Input field variants: filled, outlined, read-only — clearly differentiated
Button hierarchy: primary, secondary, ghost, destructive
examples: Form where editable fields have a visible border and read-only values are plain text on a tinted background.
Action area where 'Save' is filled primary colour and 'Cancel' uses a ghost treatment.
principles.designPrompt: Define a strict visual language: one style per role. Never mix.

principles.name: Figure-Ground
principles.summary: The brain automatically separates visual scenes into a subject and its background.
principles.description: In UI, the figure is the content users must act on; the ground is structural scaffolding — grids, containers, chrome. When the ground is too prominent, users must work to extract the figure. Heavy grid lines and coloured backgrounds risk becoming figure, competing with content.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing data tables, dashboards, and any content-dense surface where content competes with structure.
principles.whyItMatches: This explains why removing grid lines from tables often improves readability — it restores data as figure and demotes structure to ground.

actions.title: Make content the visual foreground
actions.description: Ensure data values, labels, and actions are more visually prominent than the containers and lines around them.

actions.title: Reduce structural chrome
actions.description: Use subtle borders, faint dividers, and low-contrast backgrounds to keep structural elements in the background.

actions.title: Reserve background colour for grouping not decoration
actions.description: Only use background fills when they communicate a meaningful grouping or state.

antiPatterns: Heavy grid lines in data tables competing with cell values
Strongly coloured section backgrounds overpowering the content
Decorative patterns or textures in content areas
uiPatterns: Borderless tables with row separation via spacing and subtle zebra-striping
Card backgrounds only 1-2 tones away from the page background
Data labels in high contrast, chrome in low contrast
examples: Results table where cell values are at 100% opacity and grid lines are at 15% opacity on white.
Dashboard panel where the KPI number is the visual anchor and the panel border is barely perceptible.
principles.designPrompt: What is the figure on this screen? Make it unambiguous before anything else.

principles.name: Law of Prägnanz
principles.summary: The brain interprets ambiguous stimuli in the simplest, most regular way possible.
principles.description: When layouts are irregular or complex without reason, the brain expends effort resolving the ambiguity. Simple, regular, symmetric compositions are processed faster and with less effort. This is not a mandate for monotony — it is a principle of purposeful complexity.
principles.whenToUse: Use when reviewing layout decisions, component shapes, and icon design for unnecessary complexity.
principles.whyItMatches: Prägnanz explains why 'clean' interfaces feel easier to use — regularity and simplicity reduce the perceptual work of parsing structure.

actions.title: Default to regular, symmetric layouts
actions.description: Use grid-aligned compositions as the baseline; deviate only when asymmetry communicates hierarchy.

actions.title: Reduce shape complexity in icons
actions.description: Use the simplest geometric form that communicates the concept — avoid decorative detail that adds no meaning.

actions.title: Eliminate non-functional visual variation
actions.description: Remove size, colour, or spacing variation that does not communicate a meaningful distinction.

antiPatterns: Arbitrary asymmetric layouts with no visual hierarchy payoff
Icons with unnecessary geometric complexity
Varied component sizes with no consistent meaning
uiPatterns: Grid-aligned card layouts with consistent dimensions
Icon sets using a shared geometric grammar
Consistent spacing multiples throughout the layout
examples: Dashboard grid where all metric cards share the same width and internal padding, variation only in content.
Icon set designed on a consistent 24px optical grid with minimal stroke variation.
principles.designPrompt: Every layout decision: is this simpler than the alternative? Default to simple.

principles.name: Law of Closure
principles.summary: The brain fills in missing information to complete familiar shapes and patterns.
principles.description: Users understand truncated text, incomplete borders, and clipped elements without needing to see the complete form. This means designers can imply boundaries without drawing them and trust users to complete partial patterns.
principles.whenToUse: Use when deciding whether to draw explicit borders, truncate content, or indicate overflow — closure often allows lighter-weight solutions.
principles.whyItMatches: Closure enables removal of redundant visual structure, supporting Prägnanz through lighter, cleaner layouts.

actions.title: Use truncation to signal overflow
actions.description: Use ellipsis or fading text edges to indicate more content — users understand without full visibility.

actions.title: Imply containers without full borders
actions.description: A partial rule or subtle background can define a group without a complete bounding box.

actions.title: Trust users to complete partial patterns
actions.description: Do not over-explain visible but partially obscured UI states.

antiPatterns: Cutting off text without any truncation signal
Heavy bounding boxes where subtle treatment suffices
Hiding overflow entirely with no signal that more content exists
uiPatterns: Card carousels with partially visible next card
Fade-to-white truncation for long-form text
List items with ellipsis and 'show more' affordance
examples: Horizontal scroll list where the last visible card is half-cut, signalling scrollability without extra controls.
Long table cell that truncates with ellipsis and shows full content on hover.
principles.designPrompt: Trust users to complete partial patterns. Don't over-explain the obvious.

principles.name: Law of Continuity
principles.summary: The eye follows smooth, continuous lines rather than abrupt changes in direction.
principles.description: Visual flow created by lines, alignment, and directional cues guides users through content without explicit wayfinding instructions. Step progressors, reading flows, and data tables all benefit from continuity cues that direct attention along the intended path.
principles.whenToUse: Use in stepper flows, onboarding sequences, and multi-column layouts where visual direction matters.
principles.whyItMatches: Continuity reduces wayfinding effort by making the intended path obvious through visual structure rather than instruction.

actions.title: Use alignment to imply reading direction
actions.description: Left-align content in left-to-right reading cultures to create a strong scan line.

actions.title: Connect step progression with visual lines
actions.description: Link step indicators with connecting lines to communicate sequential flow.

actions.title: Maintain column alignment across sections
actions.description: Ensure consistent vertical alignment so the eye can move smoothly down a column.

antiPatterns: Step indicators without connecting lines, making order ambiguous
Multi-column layouts with inconsistent internal alignment
Abrupt section breaks with no visual transition cue
uiPatterns: Numbered stepper with connecting progress line
Left-aligned content grid with consistent vertical rhythm
Timeline components with continuous vertical axis
examples: Checkout stepper showing a horizontal connector line between numbered steps.
Audit timeline where entries are connected by a vertical line emphasising chronological continuity.
principles.designPrompt: Use connecting visual elements to imply flow continuity across steps.

principles.name: Law of Common Fate
principles.summary: Elements that move together are perceived as belonging to the same group.
principles.description: Shared motion communicates grouping more powerfully than static proximity or similarity. When related items animate in synchrony — collapsing, fading, or highlighting together — motion performs grouping work without adding visual structure.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing interactive states, animations, and transitions where grouping needs to be communicated dynamically.
principles.whyItMatches: Motion-based grouping communicates relationships that would otherwise require additional structural elements.

actions.title: Move related items together in transitions
actions.description: When collapsing or expanding, animate items in the same group in synchrony.

actions.title: Use hover states that highlight entire groups
actions.description: Ensure row hover and selection states highlight all elements in a group simultaneously.

actions.title: Animate filtering to show category membership
actions.description: When filters are applied, animate matching items together while others fade.

antiPatterns: Items from the same group animating at different speeds or directions
Hover states that only highlight one element of a multi-element group
Transitions that obscure rather than communicate grouping
uiPatterns: Row highlight on hover covering icon, label, and action button together
Filter chip group that collapses as a unit
Card selection animation moving selected cards together
examples: Data table where hovering a row highlights all cells simultaneously, reinforcing they belong together.
Tag filter where removing a category collapses all tags in that category with a shared motion.
principles.designPrompt: Use consistent motion direction to communicate object relationships.

principles.name: Law of Symmetry
principles.summary: Symmetric compositions are perceived as unified, stable, and easier to process.
principles.description: Symmetric layouts — balanced columns, consistent card sizes, mirrored panel layouts — are processed with less perceptual effort. Asymmetry is a tool for communicating hierarchy; used without purpose it simply increases cognitive cost.
principles.whenToUse: Use in card grids, comparison layouts, and any surface where visual balance supports equal-weight content.
principles.whyItMatches: Symmetric structures allow the brain to process layout as a single unit rather than resolving individual element relationships.

actions.title: Use consistent card dimensions in grids
actions.description: Give cards equal width and height when they represent items of equal rank.

actions.title: Mirror layouts for comparison content
actions.description: In side-by-side comparison views, use identical structural templates for each option.

actions.title: Reserve asymmetry for hierarchy
actions.description: Use asymmetric layout only when one side carries more visual weight by design.

antiPatterns: Cards of varying sizes in a grid without meaningful reason
Comparison layouts with different structural templates on each side
Arbitrary visual imbalance in content areas
uiPatterns: Fixed-dimension card grids for equal-rank content
Symmetric two-column comparison layout
Balanced header/footer proportions
examples: Plan comparison page with three equal-width cards, each using the same internal layout.
Side-by-side document review where both panels use identical structural templates.
principles.designPrompt: Default to symmetric layouts. Add asymmetry only for deliberate emphasis.

principles.name: Loss Aversion
principles.summary: Losses feel approximately twice as painful as equivalent gains feel good.
principles.description: Loss aversion explains why users over-attend to the risks of acting and underattend to the costs of not acting. Irreversible actions cause anxiety, deletion warnings are highly effective, and loss-framed messages carry disproportionate weight in decisions.
principles.whenToUse: Use in consent flows, destructive action confirmations, cancellation flows, and risk communication.
principles.whyItMatches: Loss framing often doubles the weight users give to objective information — misuse causes unnecessary anxiety; correct use improves informed decision-making.

actions.title: Make destructive actions reversible
actions.description: Use soft delete, undo windows, and recovery options to reduce the felt cost of action.

actions.title: Use loss framing carefully in risk communication
actions.description: Present potential downsides with equal weight to benefits in consent and risk disclosure contexts.

actions.title: Signal reversibility at the point of decision
actions.description: When an action can be undone, say so clearly at the confirmation step to reduce anxiety.

antiPatterns: Irreversible destructive actions with no undo or recovery
Consent forms that foreground benefits and bury risks
Cancellation flows designed to maximise anxiety rather than support informed choice
uiPatterns: Trash with 30-day recovery period instead of immediate deletion
Undo toast after destructive actions
Balanced risk-benefit summary in consent flows
examples: Account deletion flow showing a 30-day recovery window and summarising what will be lost.
Subscription cancellation stating 'Your data is saved for 30 days' rather than only emphasising loss.
principles.designPrompt: Reframe destructive actions as protecting something, not losing something.

principles.name: Default Effect
principles.summary: Most users accept the pre-selected default option rather than actively changing it.
principles.description: Defaults are the most powerful nudge in choice architecture — they set the outcome for the majority of users who do not actively change them. In regulated and high-stakes contexts, defaults must be safety-defensible, transparent, and easy to override.
principles.whenToUse: Use in any form, settings panel, or workflow where a pre-selected state exists.
principles.whyItMatches: The gap between the rate of default acceptance and active choice is almost always larger than designers expect.

actions.title: Audit every default for appropriateness
actions.description: Ensure each pre-selected option is the safest and most appropriate for the modal user.

actions.title: Make defaults transparent
actions.description: Label pre-selected options as 'Recommended' or 'Default' so users understand what was chosen for them.

actions.title: Make changing defaults frictionless
actions.description: Defaults must be easy to override — friction in changing a default is an ethical concern.

antiPatterns: Privacy settings that default to maximum data sharing
Hidden pre-checked boxes in sign-up flows
Defaults chosen for business benefit rather than user appropriateness
uiPatterns: Clearly labelled 'Recommended' pre-selection
Transparent default explanation tooltip
Opt-out design with visible, unfriction-ed change path
examples: Notification settings defaulting to essential-only with clear opt-in to more frequent updates.
Dosage selector defaulting to the evidence-based first-line option with a visible 'Change' affordance.
principles.designPrompt: Set defaults that serve 80% of users. Make changing the default easy but non-default.

principles.name: Anchoring Effect
principles.summary: People give disproportionate weight to the first number or reference they encounter.
principles.description: The first number, price, or estimate users see becomes their reference point for all subsequent judgements. Anchoring improves decision quality when reference points are appropriate (evidence-based benchmarks), or impairs it when they are arbitrary.
principles.whenToUse: Use in pricing displays, numerical input fields, risk communication, and any context where reference values are shown.
principles.whyItMatches: Anchoring is highly reliable and difficult to overcome consciously — designers control anchors more than users can resist them.

actions.title: Use evidence-based reference points
actions.description: When showing benchmarks or averages, use values grounded in data rather than chosen for persuasion.

actions.title: Show range context for numerical inputs
actions.description: Display typical ranges or reference values alongside numeric entry fields to guide estimation.

actions.title: Audit price displays for manipulative ordering
actions.description: Review whether highest prices are presented first to anchor perception of value.

antiPatterns: Showing artificially inflated original prices beside discounted prices
Numerical inputs with no indication of typical or safe ranges
Leading with an extreme value to make a subsequent value seem reasonable by comparison
uiPatterns: Range indicator beside numeric input fields
Reference range displayed alongside data values
Benchmark comparison anchored to population norms
examples: Dose entry field showing the typical dose range as placeholder text to anchor input expectations.
Budget tool showing median spend for similar organisations as context before input.
principles.designPrompt: Always show a reference number first. Let users orient before they decide.

principles.name: Framing Effect
principles.summary: Identical information presented differently leads to different choices.
principles.description: A 90% survival rate and a 10% mortality rate contain the same information but produce meaningfully different responses. Balanced framing — presenting both gain and loss frames — produces better-informed decisions.
principles.whenToUse: Use in consent flows, risk communication, treatment comparison, and any context where framing could bias an important decision.
principles.whyItMatches: Small wording changes produce large differences in decision outcomes — framing is one of the most reliably demonstrated effects in behavioural science.

actions.title: Present both gain and loss frames
actions.description: Show survival and mortality rates, probability of success and failure, benefit and risk side by side.

actions.title: Use natural frequencies over percentages
actions.description: Express probabilities as '1 in 20 people' rather than '5%' to improve genuine comprehension.

actions.title: Audit copy for unintentional framing bias
actions.description: Review CTAs, benefit summaries, and risk warnings for framing asymmetry.

antiPatterns: Consent forms presenting benefits prominently and risks in footnotes
Success probabilities without corresponding failure probabilities
Risk communication using only percentages without natural frequency equivalents
uiPatterns: Balanced outcome display: probability of X and probability of not-X
Natural frequency panel in risk communication flows
Side-by-side benefit and risk presentation
examples: Drug consent form showing '90 in 100 patients respond' and '10 in 100 experience side effects' with equal visual weight.
Insurance comparison showing both cost savings and coverage gaps for each plan.
principles.designPrompt: Test positive vs negative framing for every critical message. Choose intentionally.

principles.name: Status Quo Bias
principles.summary: People prefer the current state and disproportionately resist changing it.
principles.description: Users perceive any deviation from the current state as a potential loss. This explains resistance to UI migrations, settings changes, and workflow updates — even when the change is objectively beneficial.
principles.whenToUse: Use when planning migrations, introducing new workflows, or designing settings changes that affect established user behaviour.
principles.whyItMatches: Status quo bias explains why even clearly better UX can face adoption resistance — change itself is the barrier, not the quality of the change.

actions.title: Provide graceful migration paths
actions.description: Allow users to continue old workflows briefly while learning new ones, rather than hard cutoffs.

actions.title: Emphasise continuity not disruption
actions.description: Frame changes as improvements to familiar patterns rather than replacements of them.

actions.title: Reduce the activation cost of adoption
actions.description: Make the new path require fewer steps than the old one so inertia works in favour of the change.

antiPatterns: Forcing immediate adoption with no transition period
Framing changes as replacements rather than improvements
Requiring more effort to adopt the new workflow than to continue the old one
uiPatterns: Side-by-side old and new workflow comparison during migration
Gradual rollout with opt-in preview before mandatory switch
Persistent 'what changed' summary for returning users
examples: Navigation redesign offering a 30-day opt-in preview before the old layout is retired.
Workflow migration that allows users to run old and new processes in parallel for one release cycle.
principles.designPrompt: Preserve familiar patterns when redesigning. Change one thing at a time.

principles.name: Availability Heuristic
principles.summary: People judge the likelihood of events by how easily examples come to mind.
principles.description: After a highly publicised incident, users overestimate its probability; for rare but serious risks they have not encountered, they underestimate it. Dashboards and decision tools must present base-rate data, not only recent or salient cases.
principles.whenToUse: Use in monitoring dashboards, risk communication, and decision support tools where event frequency information matters.
principles.whyItMatches: This heuristic explains why salient recent events dominate risk assessment even when statistical base rates tell a different story.

actions.title: Show base-rate frequencies alongside recent events
actions.description: Contextualise recent incidents with historical frequency data so users do not over-weight the recent.

actions.title: Normalise risk using absolute numbers
actions.description: Express rare risk as '1 occurrence in 10,000 cases' not '0.01%' to improve calibration.

actions.title: Design decision support that surfaces statistical context
actions.description: Provide historical trends and base rates wherever point-in-time data is shown.

antiPatterns: Monitoring dashboards showing only recent events with no historical baseline
Risk communications using only percentages without frequency context
Alert systems that amplify recent incidents without frequency normalisation
uiPatterns: Trend sparklines beside current-value metrics
Historical baseline comparison in alert detail panels
Base-rate callout in risk disclosure flows
examples: Safety dashboard showing incident count alongside historical average to contextualise current period data.
Drug side-effect disclosure showing absolute frequency (e.g., '3 in 1,000 patients') rather than only a percentage.
principles.designPrompt: Treat session history as a promise. If you showed it once, users expect it always.

principles.name: Representativeness Heuristic
principles.summary: People judge probability by how well something matches a typical prototype.
principles.description: Users rapidly classify interface states, records, and alerts based on superficial resemblance to familiar patterns. This can be harnessed by making correct classifications obvious through visual prototypes, or it can mislead when atypical cases look like typical ones.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing status indicators, case classification, alert triage, and any UI requiring rapid categorisation.
principles.whyItMatches: This heuristic explains why atypical presentations of serious conditions are missed — they don't look like the prototype users have learned to recognise.

actions.title: Design status indicators from user prototypes
actions.description: Make critical states look like what users already associate with severity, not what the data model dictates.

actions.title: Surface atypical presentations explicitly
actions.description: When a serious case has an unusual presentation, flag it explicitly rather than relying on visual recognition.

actions.title: Validate classification UI with realistic test cases
actions.description: Test with both typical and atypical examples to ensure the interface supports correct classification across both.

antiPatterns: Alert styles that only match typical critical presentations, not atypical ones
Classification UIs tested only with idealised examples
Status indicators designed from data model logic rather than user mental models
uiPatterns: Explicit severity indicator regardless of presentation type
Atypical flag or secondary alert in classification tools
Classification validation with realistic edge-case examples
examples: Diagnostic decision support that flags 'atypical presentation' for cases that match criteria but lack typical features.
Triage tool tested with cases across the full distribution of presentations, not only textbook examples.
principles.designPrompt: Design every warning for the user who believes it doesn't apply to them.

principles.name: Decoy Effect
principles.summary: Adding a third inferior option shifts preference toward a target option.
principles.description: When a third option is clearly inferior to one of two alternatives but not the other, it shifts users toward the 'dominant' option without changing objective value. This is widely used in pricing design and can be used ethically to guide users toward better outcomes.
principles.whenToUse: Use in pricing pages, plan comparison, and any decision between options where one is genuinely better for most users.
principles.whyItMatches: The decoy effect is a reliable, well-documented mechanism that shapes choices without adding information.

actions.title: Design comparison sets that guide toward the best option
actions.description: If one plan is genuinely best for most users, structure options so it is clearly dominant.

actions.title: Avoid using the decoy effect to promote inferior outcomes
actions.description: Do not deploy asymmetric dominance to push users toward higher-cost options that are not actually better for them.

actions.title: Test option sets for unintended decoy dynamics
actions.description: Audit pricing and plan comparisons to ensure no unintended option clustering biases choice.

antiPatterns: Pricing tiers designed primarily to make mid-tier look reasonable rather than to represent genuine value
Option sets where the decoy guides users toward the most expensive rather than most appropriate option
Comparison tables with no clear recommended option
uiPatterns: Clearly marked 'Recommended for most users' plan
Feature comparison highlighting the dominant option
Three-option set with the target option in the middle
examples: Subscription page where a mid-tier plan is the recommended default and its feature set clearly dominates the basic option.
Storage tier comparison where the middle option is highlighted as best value based on typical usage patterns.
principles.designPrompt: Structure pricing or option tiers with an asymmetrically dominated middle option.

principles.name: Planning Fallacy
principles.summary: People systematically underestimate the time, costs, and risks of future tasks.
principles.description: Users entering time estimates, deadlines, and resource requirements will almost always under-provide. Interfaces that accept estimates without challenge or reference data systematically inherit this optimism bias.
principles.whenToUse: Use in scheduling tools, project planning, time-entry forms, and any UI where users provide estimates of effort or duration.
principles.whyItMatches: Planning fallacy is a near-universal bias — accepting raw estimates without correction builds systematic under-allocation into downstream plans.

actions.title: Show historical estimates alongside input fields
actions.description: Display the user's own past estimates and actuals when they enter new ones to improve calibration.

actions.title: Surface reference class data
actions.description: Show typical durations for similar tasks to anchor estimates in base-rate reality.

actions.title: Prompt for risk contingency
actions.description: Ask explicitly whether the estimate includes buffer for unexpected delays.

antiPatterns: Time-entry fields with no historical or reference context
Accepting deadline inputs without surfacing past performance data
Project planning UIs that never challenge optimistic estimates
uiPatterns: Inline historical average beside estimate input
Reference class tooltip for common task types
Contingency buffer prompt in project scheduling flows
examples: Sprint planning tool showing each team's historical velocity beside their new estimate input.
Project scheduling form that displays median delivery time for similar past projects alongside the deadline field.
principles.designPrompt: Add honest time estimates to every multi-step process. Under-promise, over-deliver.

principles.name: Dual Process Theory
principles.summary: Cognition operates through a fast, automatic system and a slow, deliberate one.
principles.description: System 1 is fast, intuitive, and pattern-driven; System 2 is slow, effortful, and analytical. Most UX decisions engage System 1 by default. High-stakes decisions require interfaces that interrupt System 1 and force System 2 engagement — without interrupting it for low-stakes routine tasks.
principles.whenToUse: Use when deciding whether a decision point warrants friction (to engage System 2) or fluency (to support System 1).
principles.whyItMatches: This framework explains why the same interface design principle — reduce friction — is correct for routine tasks and dangerous for high-stakes irreversible ones.

actions.title: Add friction selectively for high-stakes actions
actions.description: Force a deliberate pause — confirmation, summary, or delay — only for actions that are consequential and hard to reverse.

actions.title: Remove friction for routine tasks
actions.description: Make repetitive low-stakes tasks as fast and fluent as possible to support System 1 efficiency.

actions.title: Design decision quality into the interface
actions.description: For complex decisions, surface the key criteria and risks before the user commits, not after.

antiPatterns: High-friction confirmations for trivial, reversible actions
One-click irreversible destructive actions with no pause
Complex clinical decisions surfaced as simple binary choices
uiPatterns: Confirmation modal with decision summary for irreversible high-stakes actions
Optimistic, instant UI for low-stakes repeated tasks
Decision support panel surfacing key criteria before commit
examples: Drug order interface requiring explicit dose confirmation for high-risk medications but not for routine reorders.
File delete that is instant with undo toast; permanent delete requires typing 'DELETE' to confirm.
principles.designPrompt: Map each screen task to System 1 or System 2. Reduce System 2 requirements relentlessly.

principles.name: Neural Habituation
principles.summary: Repeated exposure to a stimulus causes diminishing neural response — users stop noticing it.
principles.description: Alerts, banners, and notifications that fire repeatedly with low signal-to-noise lose their effectiveness as the nervous system habituates to them. This is the neurological root cause of alert fatigue and banner blindness.
principles.whenToUse: Use when auditing notification frequency, alert policies, and any system that uses persistent or repeated visual signals.
principles.whyItMatches: Habituation is a pre-attentive neurological process — no amount of user training overcomes it. The only fix is reducing stimulus frequency.

actions.title: Reduce alert frequency radically
actions.description: Only fire an alert when action is genuinely required — every spurious alert reduces future alert effectiveness.

actions.title: Vary presentation of important signals
actions.description: Change the visual form of high-priority alerts occasionally to prevent habituation to a fixed pattern.

actions.title: Audit alert-to-action ratios
actions.description: Measure what percentage of fired alerts result in user action; target >80% for critical alerts.

antiPatterns: Informational banners displayed continuously on every page visit
Notification systems with no suppression for users who consistently dismiss
Alert systems where >50% of alerts require no action
uiPatterns: Alert suppression after repeated dismissal without action
Tiered notification policy with strict criteria for each severity level
Periodic audit dashboard showing alert-to-action ratios
examples: Monitoring system that automatically suppresses recurring non-actionable alerts after 3 consecutive dismissals.
Security platform that escalates only when a threshold of related events is crossed, not on every individual event.
principles.designPrompt: High-priority alerts: rare and prominent. Low-priority: suppressible after 3 dismissals.

principles.name: Attentional Spotlight
principles.summary: Attention operates like a spotlight: it illuminates one region at a time and suppresses the periphery.
principles.description: The brain actively suppresses processing outside the current attentional focus. This means dense interfaces with many competing regions force constant spotlight shifts, increasing cognitive cost and reducing accuracy.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing dashboards, data tables, and monitoring interfaces where users must scan and focus in sequence.
principles.whyItMatches: Every extra competing region in a dense UI increases the cost of shifting and redirecting the attentional spotlight.

actions.title: Reduce simultaneous competing focal regions
actions.description: Limit the number of distinct attention anchors on a single view to the minimum required.

actions.title: Use visual direction cues to guide the spotlight
actions.description: Apply size, contrast, and position hierarchy to sequence where attention flows.

actions.title: Support focused review modes
actions.description: Provide a single-item or detail view that removes peripheral items while a user reviews a specific record.

antiPatterns: Dashboards with 10+ equal-weight metric panels competing for attention
No clear hierarchy directing where to look first
Inline editing that forces the user to context-switch across multiple focus regions simultaneously
uiPatterns: Progressive detail: summary list expanding to focused single-item view
Visual hierarchy that establishes a clear first, second, third attention stop
Side panel focus mode that dims the list while a record is open
examples: Alert dashboard that sorts by severity so the top item always anchors attention first.
Record review mode that dims the list column while the detail panel is active.
principles.designPrompt: On every screen, where does the eye go first? There should be exactly one answer.

principles.name: Emotional Memory Encoding
principles.summary: Emotionally significant events are encoded in memory more strongly than neutral ones.
principles.description: The amygdala enhances consolidation of emotionally arousing experiences — both positive and negative. Interfaces that create appropriate emotional resonance at key moments improve retention and recall of important information.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding, risk communication, and key milestone moments where retention of information or emotional association with the product matters.
principles.whyItMatches: Neutral, clinical interfaces may be accurate but unmemorable; emotionally resonant design at the right moments can significantly improve retention of critical information.

actions.title: Design emotionally resonant completion moments
actions.description: Create moments of genuine satisfaction or meaning at key task completions to strengthen positive memory encoding.

actions.title: Use appropriate emotional weight for risk communication
actions.description: Risk disclosures that are too dry fail to encode; those that are too alarming cause avoidance — calibrate carefully.

actions.title: Avoid emotional manipulation
actions.description: Use emotional design to support genuine user outcomes, not to manufacture artificial urgency or attachment.

antiPatterns: Entirely neutral, clinically dry onboarding that leaves no memorable impression
Risk communication so alarming that users disengage rather than act
Emotional cues used to bypass informed decision-making
uiPatterns: Meaningful completion animations at genuine milestone moments
Conversational, warm tone in first-use experiences
Calibrated visual weight for risk disclosure — serious but not alarming
examples: Health app that uses a calm, affirming animation when a user completes their first data entry, reinforcing the habit.
Consent flow using a clear, matter-of-fact tone that is serious without being frightening.
principles.designPrompt: Test error messages emotionally. High-anxiety messages are remembered as negative experiences.

principles.name: Dopaminergic Reward System
principles.summary: The brain's reward system is most strongly activated by variable, unpredictable rewards.
principles.description: Dopaminergic neurons fire most strongly in anticipation of uncertain rewards. This explains why variable reward patterns (notifications, streaks, unlock moments) can be compelling — and why they can be used ethically to support genuine user goals or unethically to manufacture compulsion.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding, habit-forming workflows, and learning tools where sustained engagement supports genuine user outcomes.
principles.whyItMatches: Understanding reward circuitry is essential for designing motivational features that support user goals rather than exploiting neurological vulnerabilities.

actions.title: Tie rewards to genuine user milestones
actions.description: Only deploy reward mechanisms for actions that represent real progress toward the user's own goals.

actions.title: Use predictable rewards for compliance-critical tasks
actions.description: For tasks users must complete correctly, predictable positive feedback is safer than variable reward.

actions.title: Avoid dark patterns from variable reward design
actions.description: Do not use variable reward schedules to maximise time-on-product at the expense of user wellbeing.

antiPatterns: Streak mechanics that cause anxiety when broken
Notification systems calibrated for maximum dopaminergic pull rather than user benefit
Gamification that rewards engagement rather than task quality
uiPatterns: Progress milestones with genuine meaning tied to user goals
Predictable, immediate positive feedback for correct task completion
Wellbeing-conscious streak design with graceful break forgiveness
examples: Learning platform that celebrates completing a module with a genuine skill unlock, not an arbitrary badge.
Data entry tool giving immediate positive confirmation when a complex form is submitted correctly.
principles.designPrompt: Create clear, predictable milestone rewards at each step of long workflows.

principles.name: Embodied Cognition
principles.summary: Cognition is shaped by bodily experience — physical metaphors and motor patterns aid understanding.
principles.description: Understanding and memory are grounded in physical experience. Drag-to-delete, swipe-to-confirm, and physical layout metaphors (e.g., a stack of cards) leverage motor memory and embodied understanding to reduce the cognitive cost of learning interactions.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing touch interactions, drag-and-drop interfaces, and any pattern that maps to a familiar physical metaphor.
principles.whyItMatches: Interaction patterns grounded in physical metaphor are learned faster and recalled more reliably than purely abstract ones.

actions.title: Use physical metaphors for novel interactions
actions.description: Map new UI patterns to familiar physical actions — swiping a card away, stacking documents, pinching to zoom.

actions.title: Leverage motor memory for repeated actions
actions.description: Keep frequently used controls in consistent positions so muscle memory reduces deliberate attention cost.

actions.title: Test embodied patterns across input modalities
actions.description: Validate that physical metaphors work equally well with touch, mouse, and keyboard.

antiPatterns: Novel gesture patterns with no physical world equivalent
Moving control positions across versions, breaking motor memory
Purely abstract interaction models with no grounding in familiar physical experience
uiPatterns: Swipe-to-archive with physical spring-back animation
Consistent keyboard shortcut positions across all modules
Drag-and-drop reordering with visual drag shadow
