examples: Mobile triage tool using swipe-left to defer and swipe-right to action, mirroring physical card sorting.
Admin dashboard where primary actions are always anchored in the same screen position across every view.
principles.designPrompt: Map complex digital interactions to physical-world analogies.

principles.name: Colour as Cognitive Shortcut
principles.summary: The brain uses colour as a pre-attentive category cue, enabling near-instant classification.
principles.description: Colour is processed pre-attentively — before conscious attention — making it the fastest channel for communicating category and status. This power comes with constraints: colour meaning must be consistent, universal conventions must be respected, and colour alone is never sufficient for accessibility.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing status systems, severity indicators, categorical data visualisations, and any interface requiring rapid classification.
principles.whyItMatches: Pre-attentive colour processing allows status and category to be communicated in under 200ms — far faster than any other channel.

actions.title: Define a strict semantic colour system
actions.description: Assign one colour per meaning and enforce it globally — red = error, amber = warning, green = success.

actions.title: Never rely on colour alone
actions.description: Always pair colour with a text label, icon, or pattern to support colour-blind users and colour-ambiguous contexts.

actions.title: Test your colour system for cultural consistency
actions.description: Verify that your colour-to-meaning mapping holds across the cultural contexts of your user base.

antiPatterns: The same colour used for different meanings in different parts of the product
Status indicators that rely on colour alone with no text or icon backup
Using red for emphasis or decoration rather than only for error/danger
uiPatterns: Semantic colour tokens applied consistently across all components
Colour + icon + label triad for all status indicators
Accessibility test pass (WCAG AA) for all colour-coded UI elements
examples: Alert severity system where red, amber, and green each have a consistent, exclusive meaning throughout the product.
Data table where status colour is always accompanied by a text status label for colour-independent readability.
principles.designPrompt: Define a strict colour-to-meaning map. Apply it without exception across all products.

principles.name: Optimism Bias
principles.summary: People systematically believe they are less at risk than others from negative events.
principles.description: Optimism bias causes users to underweight personal risk — they know a side effect affects 1 in 100 people but believe it won't apply to them. Risk communication must be personalised and concrete to overcome this systematic self-exemption tendency.
principles.whenToUse: Use in consent flows, risk disclosure, safety-critical onboarding, and any context where users must accurately assess their own risk.
principles.whyItMatches: Generic, population-level risk statistics are the least effective format for users who automatically apply optimism bias to abstract averages.

actions.title: Personalise risk communication
actions.description: Use the user's own profile data to show how general risks apply specifically to their situation.

actions.title: Use absolute rather than relative risk
actions.description: Express risk as '10 in 100 people like you' not 'increases risk by 50%' to make probability concrete.

actions.title: Include self-assessment prompts
actions.description: Ask users to actively consider how a risk applies to them rather than presenting it passively.

antiPatterns: Generic population-level risk statistics without personal relevance
Relative risk figures without absolute frequency context
Passive risk disclosure with no engagement or acknowledgement
uiPatterns: Personalised risk summary based on user-provided profile data
Icon array (1 in 100 grid) for concrete frequency visualisation
Active acknowledgement checkbox with reflective prompt
examples: Screening consent form showing 'Based on your age and history, your personal risk is approximately X in 100' rather than general population statistics.
Safety briefing that asks 'Think about how this applies to your role' before the user can proceed.
principles.designPrompt: Design for the optimistic user who won't use your safety features. Make safeguards invisible-by-default.

principles.name: Anterior Cingulate Error Detection
principles.summary: The brain automatically detects mismatches between expected and actual outcomes.
principles.description: The anterior cingulate cortex fires when an action produces an unexpected result. This neurological error signal is the biological basis for learning from mistakes. Interface error feedback that is immediate, clear, and actionable leverages this natural error-detection system; delayed or vague feedback breaks it.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing error states, inline validation, and any system where users make and correct errors.
principles.whyItMatches: Immediate inline feedback aligns with the brain's natural error-detection timing — it fires on the mismatch, not 2 seconds later at form submit.

actions.title: Provide immediate inline validation
actions.description: Surface errors at the field level the moment the user moves away from an incorrect input, not at form submission.

actions.title: Make error messages actionable
actions.description: Every error message must tell the user what went wrong and what to do to fix it.

actions.title: Preserve correct input on error
actions.description: Never clear correct fields when one field fails validation — only highlight the specific problem.

antiPatterns: Validation only on form submit with no field-level feedback
Error messages that describe the problem in technical terms without a fix
Clearing the entire form on a single validation error
uiPatterns: On-blur inline validation with icon + message
Error summary at top of form with anchor links to each failing field
Field-level error state persisting until corrected
examples: Medication order form that validates dose range immediately when the user leaves the dose field.
Registration form that confirms each field individually so users see success as they complete it.
principles.designPrompt: Inconsistency is neurological load. Audit interaction patterns relentlessly.

principles.name: Cognitive Dissonance
principles.summary: People experience discomfort when their actions and beliefs conflict, and act to resolve it.
principles.description: After making a choice, users tend to interpret new information in ways that justify it rather than revisit it. In UX, dissonance explains post-purchase regret, resistance to error feedback that implies wrong choices, and the power of small commitments in building compliance with larger ones.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding commitment flows, behaviour change tools, and any context where users must reconcile a previous choice with new information.
principles.whyItMatches: Dissonance reduction is automatic — users will reinterpret error feedback to avoid changing a committed choice unless that feedback is unambiguous.

actions.title: Use commitment escalation strategically
actions.description: In onboarding, request small commitments that build consistency with the product before requesting larger ones.

actions.title: Acknowledge prior choices in feedback
actions.description: When an error implies a prior choice was wrong, frame correction as refinement rather than reversal.

actions.title: Make correction feel like progress
actions.description: Frame updating a decision as 'improving your answer' rather than 'you were wrong'.

antiPatterns: Error messages that imply the user made a fundamentally wrong choice without offering a path forward
Behaviour change tools that ask for large commitment from users with no prior engagement
Confrontational feedback that triggers defensiveness rather than reflection
uiPatterns: Progressive commitment ladder in onboarding (small → large ask)
Correction framed as 'update' rather than 'error'
Reconfirmation flow that validates the updated choice rather than the original
examples: Onboarding that asks for a small profile detail before requesting integration setup, building commitment progressively.
Form that says 'Update your selection' rather than 'You selected incorrectly' when a user must change a prior input.
principles.designPrompt: When breaking established patterns, always explain why. Unexplained change creates dissonance.

principles.name: Authority Bias
principles.summary: People give disproportionate weight to information from perceived authorities.
principles.description: Authority cues — credentials, institutional logos, expert endorsements — increase compliance and trust. In UX, surfacing the provenance and guidelines basis of interface recommendations can improve compliance, but fabricated or inflated authority signals erode long-term trust.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing evidence-based decision support, compliance flows, and any context where source credibility affects willingness to follow guidance.
principles.whyItMatches: Authority cues can bridge the gap between what users want to do and what evidence recommends they do — provided the authority is real.

actions.title: Surface the evidence basis for recommendations
actions.description: When the interface recommends an option, show the guideline, source, or evidence it is based on.

actions.title: Use institutional credibility appropriately
actions.description: Reference real organisations, guidelines, and evidence — do not fabricate authority.

actions.title: Allow authority cues to be inspected
actions.description: Provide links to source guidelines so users who want to verify can do so.

antiPatterns: Recommendations with no stated basis or provenance
Vague appeals to authority without verifiable references
Using authority framing to override rather than inform user judgement
uiPatterns: Guideline citation beside clinical or compliance recommendation
Source tooltip showing the evidence basis for a recommendation
Institutional badge with link to verifiable source
examples: Drug prescribing tool showing the NICE guideline reference beside the recommended first-line option.
Compliance checklist that links each requirement to the regulatory document it derives from.
principles.designPrompt: Your system is an authority. Defaults are authoritative recommendations — use that responsibility carefully.

principles.name: Reactance Theory
principles.summary: When people feel their freedom to choose is threatened, they resist — even choosing the prohibited option.
principles.description: High-friction blocks, mandatory overrides, and forced flows that remove user autonomy trigger reactance — users resist or circumvent them. Preserving user autonomy (with a clear opt-out) while nudging toward better choices is more effective than removing choice.
principles.whenToUse: Use in safety-critical workflows, compliance flows, and any design that restricts user options or imposes mandatory steps.
principles.whyItMatches: Reactance explains why hard blocks in clinical decision support are often overridden at higher rates than soft alerts — restriction triggers resistance.

actions.title: Preserve user autonomy in nudge design
actions.description: Always provide an explicit opt-out or override path — if the choice is wrong, explain why; don't block.

actions.title: Use soft alerts over hard blocks
actions.description: Present warnings and recommendations as interruptive information rather than hard gate controls.

actions.title: Frame restrictions as protections, not controls
actions.description: When a restriction genuinely protects the user, explain the reason rather than simply imposing it.

antiPatterns: Hard blocks on actions with no explanation or override path
Mandatory workflows that remove all user agency
Warnings that do not explain the reason for the constraint
uiPatterns: Soft interruptive alert with explicit 'Proceed anyway — I understand the risk' override
Friction-with-explanation modal rather than hard block
Autonomy-preserving nudge: recommended option highlighted but alternatives accessible
examples: Drug interaction alert that presents the risk and reason, then offers 'Accept risk and continue' rather than a hard block.
Budget approval flow that flags over-budget but allows an authorised user to proceed with a documented reason.
principles.designPrompt: Every mandatory field needs a micro-explanation of why it's required.

principles.name: Learned Helplessness
principles.summary: Repeated failure leads users to stop trying, even when success becomes possible.
principles.description: Users who experience repeated, unexplained errors, unsuccessful searches, or confusing interfaces learn to disengage rather than persist. Once learned helplessness sets in, even a fixed interface does not automatically recover engagement — the damage is to user confidence, not just the task.
principles.whenToUse: Use when reviewing error-dense workflows, failed search experiences, and any interface where users frequently give up or seek help.
principles.whyItMatches: Learned helplessness is cumulative — each failure event reduces future willingness to try, even when the interface improves.

actions.title: Surface partial success signals during errors
actions.description: When users fail a step, acknowledge what they got right before addressing what needs to change.

actions.title: Provide always-available recovery paths
actions.description: Ensure every dead end, error state, and failed search has a clear next step — never leave users stuck.

actions.title: Use progress indicators during long or complex tasks
actions.description: Show users how far they have come and how little remains so momentum is sustained.

antiPatterns: Error messages that describe only what failed with no path forward
Search results that return zero results with no suggestion or fallback
Long complex forms with no progress indicators
uiPatterns: Zero-results page with spelling suggestions, similar queries, and alternative paths
Error message with specific fix guidance and a help link
Step progress indicator visible throughout multi-step workflows
examples: Failed search that shows 'No exact matches — did you mean X? Or try browsing Y category.'
Multi-step form that shows '4 of 6 steps complete' with a breakdown of what remains.
principles.designPrompt: Detect repeated failures on the same step. Offer contextual help after 2 failed attempts.

principles.name: IKEA Effect
principles.summary: People value things more highly when they have invested effort in creating or configuring them.
principles.description: Users who configure, customise, or build their own setup feel greater ownership and are more invested in the outcome. Onboarding that requires users to make meaningful configuration choices increases engagement and reduces churn compared to fully automatic setup.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding flows, configuration wizards, and personalisation features where user investment can be meaningfully encouraged.
principles.whyItMatches: The IKEA effect explains why 'set it up yourself' onboarding often outperforms 'we set it up for you' onboarding in long-term engagement.

actions.title: Require meaningful configuration in onboarding
actions.description: Ask users to make at least a few real choices during setup — not trivial aesthetic preferences, but substantive decisions.

actions.title: Reflect user effort back to them
actions.description: Show users what they have configured and built so the investment is visible and reinforces ownership.

actions.title: Balance effort with reward
actions.description: Configuration effort must lead to an immediately visible outcome improvement — effort without payoff produces frustration.

antiPatterns: Fully automatic setup with no user involvement or choice
Configuration choices with no visible effect on the user's experience
Excessive setup steps that overwhelm rather than engage
uiPatterns: Personalisation wizard during onboarding with visible outcome preview
Setup completion summary showing what the user configured
Dashboard that reflects user-defined priorities and preferences
examples: Analytics tool that asks users to select their most important metrics during setup, then builds their default dashboard from those choices.
Communication platform that has users select team channels and preferences in onboarding, surfacing the personalised result immediately.
principles.designPrompt: Build meaningful customisation into complex workflows. Participation creates ownership.

principles.name: Mere Exposure Effect
principles.summary: Repeated exposure to something increases liking and trust, even without conscious awareness.
principles.description: Familiar interface conventions and patterns feel more trustworthy and usable than novel ones, even when users cannot articulate why. This is the neurological basis for Jakob's Law — familiarity reduces cognitive resistance.
principles.whenToUse: Use when evaluating novelty in design — every departure from convention must justify its cognitive cost against the familiarity benefit users lose.
principles.whyItMatches: Mere exposure explains why familiar patterns feel 'intuitive' — it is repeated exposure, not inherent simplicity, that creates ease.

actions.title: Preserve familiar conventions for core patterns
actions.description: Use standard patterns for navigation, search, forms, and alerts — innovation is best applied to content, not structure.

actions.title: Introduce novel patterns gradually
actions.description: When a novel pattern is necessary, expose users to it repeatedly in low-stakes contexts before it carries critical weight.

actions.title: Test novel patterns with first-time and returning users separately
actions.description: Familiarity effects compound over time — first-time performance does not predict long-term ease.

antiPatterns: Novel navigation patterns with no familiarity basis in common tools
Customised icons for actions that have standard iconographic conventions
Unique interaction patterns that create learning costs without offering commensurate value
uiPatterns: Convention-first navigation following platform standards
Standard icon set with universal semantic meaning
Gradual exposure to novel patterns via progressive onboarding
examples: Enterprise tool using the same navigation structure and keyboard shortcuts as the most common tool in its category.
New interaction pattern introduced as an optional 'try the new view' before it becomes the default.
principles.designPrompt: Use the most common patterns from tools your users already know. Familiarity equals perceived simplicity.

principles.name: Reciprocity Norm
principles.summary: People feel a strong obligation to return favours and helpful acts.
principles.description: Providing genuine value before asking for commitment, data, or action exploits the deeply wired reciprocity norm — users who receive something useful are more likely to engage with subsequent requests. The reverse also holds: asking before giving produces resistance.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding value delivery, freemium unlocks, data collection consent, and collaboration handover design.
principles.whyItMatches: Reciprocity is one of the most powerful social influence mechanisms — giving genuine value first is both ethically sound and strategically effective.

actions.title: Deliver value before requesting data or commitment
actions.description: Show users the product working meaningfully before asking for account creation, payment, or data sharing.

actions.title: Make help requests feel mutual
actions.description: Frame data collection as 'help us help you' with a clear and credible description of what the user gains.

actions.title: Provide generous handover context in collaborative flows
actions.description: When transferring work, include more context than strictly required — it builds trust and reduces handover friction.

antiPatterns: Sign-up walls before the user can see any product value
Data requests with no stated benefit to the user
Minimal handover notes that leave the recipient to reconstruct context
uiPatterns: Value-first onboarding: immediate demo or trial before account creation
Data consent form that clearly states what the user receives in exchange
Rich handover template prompting the sender to include context and rationale
examples: Analytics tool that lets users explore a demo workspace before requiring account creation.
Collaboration handover form that prompts 'What does the next person need to know?' with structured context fields.
principles.designPrompt: Give users something useful before asking them to do work. Help first, ask later.

principles.name: Self-Determination Theory
principles.summary: Intrinsic motivation requires autonomy, competence, and relatedness — external rewards undermine it.
principles.description: People are intrinsically motivated when they feel autonomous (in control of choices), competent (capable and progressing), and related (connected to others with shared purpose). Extrinsic rewards that replace intrinsic motivation reduce sustained engagement.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding, learning tools, and long-form collaboration platforms where sustained voluntary engagement is the goal.
principles.whyItMatches: SDT explains why gamification often produces initial engagement spikes followed by long-term disengagement — points and badges crowd out intrinsic motivation.

actions.title: Design for autonomy
actions.description: Give users meaningful choice in how they complete tasks — autonomy is more motivating than mandated workflows.

actions.title: Build in competence progression
actions.description: Structure tasks so users can visibly improve and develop skill — not just complete actions.

actions.title: Strengthen relatedness through shared context
actions.description: Show users how their work connects to team progress and shared goals.

antiPatterns: Gamification that replaces task meaning with external reward
Mandatory workflows with no user agency over process
Individual task completion with no visibility of team context or impact
uiPatterns: Flexible workflow with multiple valid completion paths
Skill progression indicator tied to meaningful capability growth
Team contribution view showing individual impact on collective goal
examples: Learning tool that shows users how their completed modules build toward a specific, self-chosen competency.
Project tool that surfaces individual contributions within the team's overall progress view.
principles.designPrompt: For every major workflow: does it give choice (autonomy), build skill (competence), and connect to others?

principles.name: Negativity Bias
principles.summary: Negative events have a disproportionately larger psychological impact than equivalent positive ones.
principles.description: A single error, bug, or system failure creates a stronger negative impression than multiple successes can compensate for. Users give errors and failures approximately 2-3× more cognitive weight than successes. This is the evolutionary basis of loss aversion.
principles.whenToUse: Use when evaluating error recovery design, trust-building patterns, and the relative cost of usability failures versus usability improvements.
principles.whyItMatches: Negativity bias means that fixing the worst experience often delivers more perceived quality improvement than adding new positive features.

actions.title: Prioritise error elimination over new feature delivery
actions.description: In product prioritisation, removing pain from bad experiences typically improves perceived quality more than adding new positives.

actions.title: Design error recovery to be faster and clearer than the error is frustrating
actions.description: The recovery experience must exceed the negative impression of the error in speed and clarity.

actions.title: Avoid first-use errors at all costs
actions.description: First impressions are set through this bias — a first-use failure can permanently affect perceived quality.

antiPatterns: New feature launches before known error states are resolved
Error recovery flows that are more complex than the error itself
Onboarding flows that surface error states before users have succeeded
uiPatterns: First-use success path: ensure no user can encounter an error on first launch
Fast, clear error recovery modal with immediate fix path
Error rate monitoring as a first-class product quality metric
examples: Checkout error that resolves in one step with a friendly explanation, recovering trust faster than the error cost it.
Product launch that gates users from any known error path until the fix is deployed.
principles.designPrompt: Map your worst-case flows. They define your product reputation more than best-case flows.

principles.name: Threat Detection Bias
principles.summary: The brain is evolutionarily tuned to detect potential threats even from ambiguous stimuli.
principles.description: Threat-related stimuli — red colour, warning icons, high-pitched tones — grab attention automatically and pre-attentively. This can be harnessed to ensure critical alerts are noticed, or misused to create false urgency and dark patterns.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing critical alert systems, safety warnings, and risk communication — and when auditing for dark patterns that misuse threat signals.
principles.whyItMatches: Threat-detection is the pre-attentive system that makes red alerts effective — misusing it for non-threats destroys the effectiveness of genuine signals.

actions.title: Reserve threat signals exclusively for genuine threats
actions.description: Red colour, warning icons, and urgent language must only be used for genuine critical states.

actions.title: Use pre-attentive threat cues to ensure critical alert visibility
actions.description: Design critical alerts to trigger automatic threat-detection — red, high-contrast, motion.

actions.title: Audit for manufactured urgency dark patterns
actions.description: Remove countdown timers, scarcity warnings, and threat language used to drive commercial decisions rather than genuine risk.

antiPatterns: Red used for promotional emphasis rather than genuine danger
Countdown timers on decisions that have no genuine time constraint
Warning icons on information that is not actually a warning
uiPatterns: Exclusive red-for-danger semantic rule in design system
Pre-attentive contrast and motion reserved for critical alerts
Audit checklist for manufactured urgency in commercial UI
examples: Security dashboard using red exclusively for active threats, amber for warnings, and blue for informational items.
Checkout flow that removes artificial countdown timers for cart expiry that do not reflect genuine inventory constraints.
principles.designPrompt: Reserve red exclusively for critical errors. Use amber for warnings.

principles.name: Face Detection Bias
principles.summary: The brain has a dedicated, over-sensitive system for detecting human faces.
principles.description: Human faces are processed preferentially and automatically — they capture attention and communicate trustworthiness. User avatars, profile images, and human-centred illustrations leverage this bias to build trust and social presence in digital interfaces.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing collaboration tools, user attribution, trust signals, and any context where human presence strengthens engagement.
principles.whyItMatches: Face presence increases trust and perceived social accountability — avatars on comments and approvals change how users interact with that content.

actions.title: Use real user avatars in collaborative contexts
actions.description: Show commenter, approver, and reviewer faces wherever attribution matters for trust and accountability.

actions.title: Use human imagery in trust-building contexts
actions.description: Human faces in onboarding and consent flows signal human involvement and accountability.

actions.title: Avoid generic placeholder avatars for named users
actions.description: Named users without faces feel anonymous — use initials with colour as a minimum fallback.

antiPatterns: Anonymous grayscale icons for named users in review and approval flows
No human presence in high-trust-requirement contexts
Generic stock imagery that reads as artificial rather than genuine
uiPatterns: Circular avatar with initials fallback for all named users
Reviewer presence indicator with face thumbnail in approval flows
Human-centred illustration style in onboarding
examples: Code review tool showing each reviewer's avatar beside their comment thread.
Consent flow signed by a named, photographed clinician rather than an anonymous department.
principles.designPrompt: If trust matters, put a human face in the interface. It activates social trust circuitry.

principles.name: Effort Heuristic
principles.summary: People judge quality and value by the apparent effort that went into something.
principles.description: Users perceive high-effort processes as producing higher quality outcomes — a short consent form feels less thorough than a longer one, a quickly generated report feels less credible than one that takes a moment to compute. This heuristic can be managed by communicating effort without manufacturing false friction.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing consent flows, generated report experiences, and pricing where perceived effort affects perceived value.
principles.whyItMatches: The effort heuristic explains why progress indicators during loading can improve perceived quality of the result — even when the computation time is fixed.

actions.title: Communicate genuine effort transparently
actions.description: During computation-heavy operations, show what is happening rather than a blank wait state.

actions.title: Avoid manufacturing false friction to signal quality
actions.description: Do not add artificial delays or unnecessary steps — communicate effort through transparency, not obstruction.

actions.title: Explain complexity in high-stakes outputs
actions.description: For generated reports or recommendations, briefly explain what was analysed to establish credibility.

antiPatterns: Blank loading screens that give no indication of what is being processed
Artificially slow loading added to make results feel more credible
Generated recommendations with no explanation of their basis
uiPatterns: Progress indicator naming what is being analysed
Processing summary panel showing inputs considered
Output provenance explanation in generated reports
examples: Risk assessment tool showing 'Analysing 47 data points across 3 frameworks...' during calculation.
AI-generated report listing the data sources and time range included in the analysis.
principles.designPrompt: In high-stakes workflows, one deliberate pause signals importance and reduces error rates.

principles.name: In-Group Bias
principles.summary: People trust and follow the behaviour of those they perceive as in their own group.
principles.description: Social proof from peers in the same role, team, or organisation is more persuasive than evidence from outsiders. Surfacing what colleagues do — rather than what the software recommends — leverages in-group trust for behaviour change and adoption.
principles.whenToUse: Use in peer-based nudges, social proof elements, and any context where adoption or compliance can be influenced by within-group norms.
principles.whyItMatches: Peer behaviour data from the same role or team is dramatically more effective than generic guidance for driving adoption and compliance.

actions.title: Show peer usage data not just global averages
actions.description: Surface what users in the same team or role do, not what all users do.

actions.title: Use team social proof for adoption nudges
actions.description: Frame feature adoption as 'X of your team members use this' rather than 'X% of users use this'.

actions.title: Attribute handover content to named team members
actions.description: Show that context was provided by a colleague to increase its credibility and uptake.

antiPatterns: Generic social proof with no role or team specificity
Adoption nudges citing global user counts to team members who identify with their local peer group
Anonymous handover notes that strip attribution and team context
uiPatterns: Team adoption bar: '4 of 6 in your team use this feature'
Peer activity feed showing same-role colleagues' recent actions
Named team member attribution on all shared content
examples: Compliance tool showing 'Your team is 85% complete — 2 members still outstanding' rather than a global percentage.
Handover note showing the previous owner's name and role to increase credibility of the context provided.
principles.designPrompt: Show team context in collaborative tools. We trust our group more than the system.

principles.name: Biophilia Effect
principles.summary: Exposure to natural forms and patterns reduces stress and restores directed attention capacity.
principles.description: Evolutionarily, the human brain finds natural patterns — organic shapes, green palettes, flowing forms — inherently restorative. In cognitively demanding interfaces, introducing biophilic visual elements reduces stress and sustains attention capacity over longer sessions.
principles.whenToUse: Use in high-load operational interfaces, long-session tools, and any product where user cognitive fatigue is a recognised problem.
principles.whyItMatches: Attention restoration theory shows measurable cognitive capacity recovery from even brief exposure to natural visual patterns.

actions.title: Introduce natural palette elements in sustained-use interfaces
actions.description: Use organic greens, warm neutrals, and soft curves as secondary elements in high-load UIs.

actions.title: Use organic shapes in illustration and iconography
actions.description: Prefer rounded, irregular forms over purely geometric ones where aesthetics allow.

actions.title: Design rest states that incorporate biophilic elements
actions.description: Empty states and loading screens are opportunities for brief restorative visual experiences.

antiPatterns: Sustained high-load interfaces with no visual respite
Purely geometric, high-contrast visual language for all-day-use tools
Empty states that feel sterile and increase rather than reduce cognitive tension
uiPatterns: Soft green secondary colour in sustained-use dashboards
Organic illustration style for empty and success states
Nature-inspired background texture in low-density areas
examples: Clinical documentation tool using a soft natural green for its completed-state indicator to provide momentary visual rest.
Empty state illustration using an organic, natural scene to signal a calm, ready state.
principles.designPrompt: Consider subtle organic shapes and muted natural tones in high-stress technical tools.

principles.name: Signal-to-Noise Ratio
principles.summary: Maximising the ratio of meaningful information to distracting noise improves comprehension speed.
principles.description: Every element in a UI that does not carry information is noise that reduces the effectiveness of elements that do. Decorative elements, redundant labels, and structural chrome all reduce signal-to-noise ratio and increase the cognitive cost of extracting meaning.
principles.whenToUse: Use as a diagnostic framework when reviewing dashboard designs, data tables, and any information-dense interface.
principles.whyItMatches: SNR is the information-theoretic basis for Tufte's data-ink ratio and the gestalt principle of Prägnanz — all three converge on removing noise to reveal signal.

actions.title: Remove non-data ink
actions.description: Eliminate gridlines, borders, backgrounds, and decorative elements that carry no data value.

actions.title: Reduce redundant labelling
actions.description: Remove axis labels, legends, and callouts that repeat information already visible in the data.

actions.title: Increase data density after removing noise
actions.description: The space freed by removing noise should increase data density, not white space alone.

antiPatterns: Dashboard panels with more decorative chrome than data content
Charts with legends, titles, axis labels, and gridlines all simultaneously visible
Tables with borders on every cell when spacing alone can separate rows
uiPatterns: Borderless table with spacing-only row separation
Chart with direct data labels instead of legend + gridlines
Dashboard where data-ink ratio exceeds 70%
examples: KPI dashboard that removes card borders, reduces gridlines to 10% opacity, and adds a sparkline for each metric.
Data table that eliminates cell borders and uses alternating subtle row tints for separation.
principles.designPrompt: For every data table: remove grid lines and colour fills unless they carry information.

principles.name: Information Hierarchy
principles.summary: Structuring information by importance speeds scanning and comprehension.
principles.description: Users scan interfaces in predictable patterns (F-shape, Z-shape) driven by visual hierarchy cues — size, weight, contrast, and position. Information that is structurally hierarchical is found faster and understood more accurately than flat lists.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing navigation structures, data tables, dashboards, and any content with multiple importance levels.
principles.whyItMatches: Visual hierarchy reduces search time by converting linear scanning into directed attention — users jump to the right level rather than reading sequentially.

actions.title: Establish a clear 3-level visual hierarchy
actions.description: Define primary, secondary, and tertiary information levels with distinct visual weights.

actions.title: Order information by user importance not system logic
actions.description: Structure screens and menus by what users need first, not by what the data model dictates.

actions.title: Use position and size to communicate importance
actions.description: The most important information should be largest, highest-contrast, and positioned at the primary scan origin.

antiPatterns: Flat lists with no visual hierarchy differentiation
Information ordered alphabetically or by system ID rather than by relevance
Equal visual weight given to primary and secondary information
uiPatterns: Card layout with headline, supporting detail, and meta-data in three distinct visual weights
Navigation ordered by frequency of use, not alphabetically
Dashboard with one dominant KPI and supporting metrics in clear visual subordination
examples: Alert list sorted by severity with critical items in a larger, bolder treatment and informational items in muted weight.
Dashboard showing primary metric at 32px bold and supporting trend data at 13px regular.
principles.designPrompt: Design three visual weight levels: large = critical, medium = supporting, small = context.

principles.name: Modality Effect
principles.summary: Learning is enhanced when information is split across visual and auditory channels rather than within a single channel.
principles.description: The brain processes visual and auditory inputs through separate cognitive channels. Presenting text and diagrams simultaneously overloads the visual channel; replacing on-screen text with narration while showing the diagram uses both channels efficiently.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing instructional content, walkthroughs, and any multi-element learning experience.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle explains why voice-over tutorial narration with visuals outperforms the same visual with on-screen caption text for complex procedural content.

actions.title: Use narration with visuals rather than on-screen text with visuals
actions.description: For instructional content, provide audio explanation alongside diagrams rather than simultaneous text.

actions.title: Avoid redundant on-screen text that repeats audio
actions.description: Text and audio covering the same content overloads the visual channel — use each for complementary content.

actions.title: Separate channels by information type
actions.description: Use visuals for spatial and relational information; use text or audio for sequential and procedural information.

antiPatterns: Tutorial with dense on-screen text and a diagram shown simultaneously
Audio narration that reads on-screen text word-for-word
Procedural instructions presented only as visual diagrams without verbal sequence
uiPatterns: Video walkthrough with voice narration and minimal on-screen text
Step-by-step tutorial using visual + spoken instruction pairing
Interactive diagram with audio tooltip rather than on-screen annotation
examples: Product walkthrough using animated visuals with concise narration instead of on-screen caption text.
Training module that uses diagrams to show relationships and narration to explain the sequence of actions.
principles.designPrompt: For complex onboarding, use audio + visual together. Complement — don't duplicate.

principles.name: Redundancy Principle
principles.summary: Adding redundant or interesting-but-irrelevant content reduces learning and comprehension.
principles.description: Extra content — interesting examples, background context, decorative illustrations, tangential information — reduces learning even when it is accurate and relevant to the topic. Each additional element competes for limited cognitive resources even when the user finds it interesting.
principles.whenToUse: Use when editing instructional content, UI copy, and any experience where removing content is considered but feels risky.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle is the empirical basis for the content editing principle 'kill your darlings' — fascinating details that do not serve the primary task reduce performance.

actions.title: Remove interesting but non-essential content
actions.description: Cut background context, supplementary examples, and interesting tangents from primary task flows.

actions.title: Audit for seductive detail in instructional UX
actions.description: Review onboarding, tutorials, and help content for elements that are interesting but not action-enabling.

actions.title: Link supplementary content rather than embedding it
actions.description: Provide links to additional context for curious users without imposing it on all users.

antiPatterns: Onboarding that includes product history or team introductions before the user has completed first use
Help documentation that leads with conceptual background before the procedural instruction
Decorative illustrations on task-completion screens that distract from the confirmation message
uiPatterns: Progressive disclosure: primary task content first, supplementary content behind 'Learn more'
Onboarding focused exclusively on first-use task completion
Help documentation leading with action, followed by optional conceptual context
examples: Setup wizard that shows only the fields needed to complete setup, with a link to advanced options for those who want them.
In-app help that starts with 'To do X: [3 steps]' and provides a 'Why does this work?' link at the bottom.
principles.designPrompt: Never use icon + label + tooltip when one suffices. Pick the right form; remove the rest.

principles.name: Zipf's Law
principles.summary: A small number of items account for the vast majority of user interactions.
principles.description: In any interface, approximately 20% of features, commands, or items are used for 80% of interactions. The remaining 80% are used rarely. Optimising the design and accessibility of the top 20% delivers disproportionate value; hiding the remaining 80% reduces cognitive cost without meaningfully reducing utility for most users.
principles.whenToUse: Use in navigation design, command palette architecture, settings organisation, and feature prioritisation.
principles.whyItMatches: Zipf's law is the information-theoretic basis for progressive disclosure — the distribution of usage almost always justifies it.

actions.title: Surface the top 20% of actions prominently
actions.description: Use analytics to identify the most frequently used features and ensure they require the fewest clicks.

actions.title: Archive the long tail behind search or advanced settings
actions.description: Move rarely used options to discoverable but non-prominent locations.

actions.title: Prioritise recents and favourites
actions.description: Give users control of their personal top-20 through recents, pinned items, and favourites.

antiPatterns: Navigation that gives equal prominence to all features regardless of usage frequency
Settings that list all options alphabetically rather than by frequency of access
Command interfaces that bury the most-used commands among rarely used ones
uiPatterns: Recents and favourites section at the top of navigation and search
Progressive disclosure: top actions prominent, full list discoverable via 'More'
Analytics-driven navigation ordering
examples: Admin panel that surfaces the 5 most-accessed reports on the homepage while archiving the full list behind search.
Settings that defaults to showing the 8 most-changed preferences with 'Show all settings' to expand.
principles.designPrompt: Run usage analytics. Surface the top 5 actions in 1 click. Deprioritise the long tail.

principles.name: Tesler's Law
principles.summary: Every application has an inherent amount of complexity that cannot be eliminated — only shifted.
principles.description: You cannot make a complex task simple — you can only decide whether the user or the system bears the complexity. Simplifying the interface by hiding complexity shifts it to the system; hiding it from users means the system must carry it correctly. When the system fails to carry it, the complexity returns to the user as unexpected errors.
principles.whenToUse: Use when evaluating simplification decisions — particularly when removing steps, hiding fields, or automating choices.
principles.whyItMatches: This law prevents simplification from becoming false simplicity — it forces explicit decisions about where complexity lives rather than assuming it can be eliminated.

actions.title: Identify where complexity is being shifted when simplifying
actions.description: For every step you remove from the user flow, confirm the system is correctly handling the complexity you absorbed.

actions.title: Never hide complexity that users must understand for safe decisions
actions.description: Some complexity is intrinsic to the domain and must remain visible — simplifying it away creates risk.

actions.title: Make system-absorbed complexity auditable
actions.description: When the interface hides complexity, provide a way for users to inspect what the system has decided on their behalf.

antiPatterns: Simplification that hides complexity without the system correctly handling it
Reducing a complex regulatory decision to a single checkbox
Automated defaults that cannot be inspected or overridden
uiPatterns: Smart defaults with 'Show what was decided automatically' disclosure
Summary view of automated decisions with one-click detail expansion
Progressive complexity: simple view by default, full control accessible
examples: Tax filing tool that automatically calculates deductions but provides a 'Show my calculations' detail panel for review.
Smart form that pre-fills fields from prior data, with each pre-fill visibly annotated as 'Pre-filled from your last submission'.

principles.name: Gricean Maxims
principles.summary: Effective communication follows four maxims: quantity, quality, relevance, and manner.
principles.description: Grice's cooperative principle holds that effective communication is: as informative as needed but not more (quantity), true and evidenced (quality), relevant to the context (relevance), and clear and unambiguous (manner). Violating any maxim creates friction, confusion, or distrust in UI copy.
principles.whenToUse: Use as a copy review framework for all user-facing strings — labels, error messages, instructions, CTAs, and confirmation messages.
principles.whyItMatches: Most UI copy failures violate at least one Gricean maxim — too much information, unverifiable claims, irrelevant context, or ambiguous wording.

actions.title: Apply quantity: say exactly enough
actions.description: Write labels, instructions, and error messages that contain all needed information and nothing extra.

actions.title: Apply quality: only state what is evidenced
actions.description: Remove marketing superlatives, unverifiable claims, and hyperbolic copy from functional UI strings.

actions.title: Apply manner: use unambiguous, ordered language
actions.description: Write instructions in active voice, chronological order, and without jargon.

antiPatterns: Help text that restates the field label without adding new information
CTAs using vague verbs like 'Continue' when the action is more specific
Error messages that describe the system's problem rather than the user's next step
uiPatterns: Field labels + placeholder + hint text each carrying distinct, non-redundant information
CTA copy that names the specific action: 'Submit expense claim' not 'Submit'
Error messages structured as: what happened + why + what to do
examples: Button labelled 'Approve and notify team' instead of 'Approve' — quantity and manner both satisfied.
Error message: 'Your session expired after 30 minutes of inactivity. Please log in to continue.' — all four maxims satisfied.
principles.designPrompt: Apply Grice to every string: Is it true? No more than needed? Relevant? Clear?

principles.name: Processing Fluency
principles.summary: Information that is easier to process is judged as more true, more trustworthy, and more credible.
principles.description: Processing fluency — how easily information can be read and understood — directly affects perceived truth and trust. High-contrast, legible typography, simple sentence structure, and familiar vocabulary all increase fluency and, consequently, credibility.
principles.whenToUse: Use in consent flows, risk communication, and any context where trust and comprehension of written content are critical.
principles.whyItMatches: The same factual content presented in low-fluency typography is rated as less credible and less believable than in high-fluency typography — a direct measure of this effect.

actions.title: Use highly legible typography for critical content
actions.description: Use a minimum 16px body font size, 4.5:1 contrast ratio, and 1.5 line-height for all consent and risk text.

actions.title: Write short, concrete sentences
actions.description: Target a maximum sentence length of 20 words for user-facing instructions and risk descriptions.

actions.title: Avoid fonts and layouts that create visual noise
actions.description: Decorative, condensed, or patterned typography backgrounds all reduce fluency and perceived credibility.

antiPatterns: Consent text in 10px light-weight font on a grey background
Long, complex sentences with embedded clauses in critical instructions
Risk disclosures in italic or condensed typefaces
uiPatterns: Consent text at 16px+ with 4.5:1 minimum contrast
Sentence-length guidance in content style guide
Fluency audit for all high-stakes user-facing strings
examples: Terms of service rewritten at Grade 8 reading level, leading to a 40% increase in actual reading and recall.
Drug consent form using 16px regular weight on white background, rated significantly more credible than the same content at 11px on grey.
principles.designPrompt: Replace any navigation label over 3 syllables with its simplest equivalent.

principles.name: Speech Act Theory
principles.summary: Language performs actions — UI copy can instruct, commit, declare, or request depending on its form.
principles.description: Speech Act Theory classifies language by what it does: directives (instructions), commissives (commitments), declarations (state changes), and expressives (emotional acknowledgements). UI copy that mismatches its speech act type to its context creates confusion — a directive framed as a declaration, or a commitment framed as a simple label.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing button labels, confirmation messages, instruction copy, and any UI string where the intent of the text must be precisely communicated.
principles.whyItMatches: UI copy that clearly performs the right speech act reduces decision time and error — users know immediately whether they are being asked to do something or informed that something happened.

actions.title: Use directives for instructional copy
actions.description: Write instructions as commands: 'Enter your date of birth' not 'Date of birth should be entered here'.

actions.title: Use declaratives for state-change confirmations
actions.description: Confirm completed actions as declarations: 'Your request has been submitted.' not 'Submit complete'.

actions.title: Use commissives for commitment CTAs
actions.description: CTAs that commit the user to an action should use first-person: 'I agree to the terms' not just 'Agree'.

antiPatterns: Instructions written in passive voice that obscure who must act
Confirmation messages that read like instructions
CTA labels that are nouns rather than verbs: 'Submission' instead of 'Submit'
uiPatterns: Imperative verb CTAs: 'Approve', 'Submit claim', 'Confirm appointment'
Declarative confirmation messages: 'Your password has been updated.'
First-person consent commitments: 'I confirm I have read and understood the above.'
examples: Consent checkbox using 'I confirm I have read the privacy policy' (commissive) rather than 'Privacy policy accepted' (ambiguous declaration).
Form instruction written as 'Upload a photo of your ID document' (directive) rather than 'ID document photo upload required' (nominalized, passive).
principles.designPrompt: Audit every CTA label: what speech act does it perform? Is that the right one?

principles.name: Prototype Theory
principles.summary: People understand categories through the most typical member, not logical definitions.
principles.description: Users do not classify by rule — they classify by resemblance to a prototype (the most typical member of a category). Navigation labels, filter categories, and content classification systems that match prototypical examples are found faster than those built from logical definitions.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing navigation labels, filter categories, content taxonomies, and any classification system users must navigate.
principles.whyItMatches: This explains why card sorting sessions reveal very different category structures than what engineers or product managers expect — user categories are built from prototypes, not logic.

actions.title: Use card sorting to identify user-built prototypes
actions.description: Conduct card sorting to discover which items users treat as prototypical members of each category before naming them.

actions.title: Name categories after their most typical member
actions.description: Use the prototypical example as the label if it communicates category membership better than an abstract noun.

actions.title: Validate taxonomy labels with representative users
actions.description: Test navigation labels by asking users to predict what they will find under each one.

antiPatterns: Navigation categories named from the data model rather than user mental models
Taxonomies built by experts without user prototype validation
Filter labels that use technical terminology users do not map to expected content
uiPatterns: Card-sort-validated navigation labels
Category examples shown in parentheses beside ambiguous labels
Faceted search with prototype-based filter naming
examples: Navigation item labelled 'Reports & analytics' changed to 'Performance reports' after card sorting revealed users used 'performance' as their prototypical category anchor.
Filter category renamed from 'Asynchronous communication tools' to 'Messaging apps' based on prototype testing.
principles.designPrompt: For every category: what is the prototypical example your user imagines? Lead with it.

principles.name: Garden Path Effect
principles.summary: Sentences that lead users toward one interpretation before revealing a different one require costly mental backtracking.
principles.description: Garden path sentences cause the reader to commit to an initial parsing that turns out to be wrong, requiring them to reparse. In UI copy, this occurs when instructions or labels appear to mean one thing until the end, then require re-reading. This increases cognitive load and error rate.
principles.whenToUse: Use when reviewing instruction copy, confirmation messages, and form labels for ambiguity that resolves late.
principles.whyItMatches: Garden path structures are common in complex instructions and legal copy — and they are directly responsible for users misunderstanding what is being asked of them.

actions.title: Front-load the most important information
actions.description: In instructions and labels, place the critical meaning at the start of the sentence, not the end.

actions.title: Test copy with first-reading comprehension
actions.description: Ask users to explain what an instruction means after reading it once — garden path failures appear immediately.

actions.title: Avoid embedded clauses in instructions
actions.description: Break complex sentences with embedded conditions into sequential simple sentences.

antiPatterns: Instructions with the key condition at the end: 'Complete this section only if you are a registered pharmacist'
Labels that appear complete but have a qualifying modifier that changes their meaning
Confirmation messages where the outcome is buried after a lengthy preamble
uiPatterns: Conditional instructions front-loaded: 'If you are a registered pharmacist, complete this section'
Confirmation message leading with outcome: 'Submitted successfully. Your manager will be notified.'
Label + qualifier pattern: '[Critical] Complete before submission' rather than 'Must be completed before submitting'
examples: Warning rewritten from 'This action, while reversible within 30 days, permanently deletes your archived data' to 'Archived data will be permanently deleted. The rest of your account can be recovered within 30 days.'
Form section header changed from 'Fields required only for non-EU residents' to 'Non-EU residents only: complete these fields'.
principles.designPrompt: Read every destructive-action dialog aloud. Does it lead users to the right conclusion first time?

principles.name: Markedness Theory
principles.summary: Unmarked (default) forms are processed faster than marked (exceptional) forms.
principles.description: In language, the unmarked form is the default — 'doctor' is the base form, 'female doctor' is marked. In UI, unmarked interface states are processed faster than marked ones. Labels, options, and states that require no qualifier are cognitively cheaper than those that do. Every qualifier adds processing cost.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing option labels, status indicators, and any UI element that distinguishes a default state from an exception.
principles.whyItMatches: This principle explains why the most common option should be presented with the simplest label — adding qualifiers to the default case increases processing cost unnecessarily.

actions.title: Use the shortest label for the most common case
actions.description: The default or most frequent state should have the simplest, qualifier-free label.

actions.title: Add qualifiers only to non-default states
actions.description: Exception states, rare options, and edge cases should carry the qualifiers — not the common case.

actions.title: Audit option sets for inverted markedness
actions.description: Review any label set where the common case has a longer or more complex label than the exception.

antiPatterns: Default option labelled 'Standard (most common)' while the exception is simply 'Advanced'
Common case requiring a qualifier while the rare exception has the simple name
Status labels where the normal state is more complex than the abnormal state
uiPatterns: Unmarked default option: the most-used choice has the simplest label
Exception badge: rare options carry a visual or textual qualifier, defaults do not
Status system where 'Normal' is the baseline and all exceptions are marked
examples: Shipping options where 'Standard delivery' is the shortest label and 'Express (next day)' carries the qualifier.
Status system where healthy/normal states show no label and all non-normal states carry a descriptor.
principles.designPrompt: Set the unmarked (neutral) form as default. Filtered or exceptional states are the marked form.

principles.name: Distributed Cognition
principles.summary: Cognition is distributed across people, artefacts, and environments — not just individual minds.
principles.description: Complex tasks are performed through systems of people and artefacts that together carry cognitive work no individual could manage alone. Interfaces that treat cognitive load as a purely individual problem miss the systemic perspective — the right external representations, shared records, and artefacts can reduce individual cognitive demand dramatically.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing collaborative workflows, shared records, and any system where teams must coordinate complex distributed tasks.
principles.whyItMatches: Distributed cognition explains why checklist artefacts, shared dashboards, and structured handover templates outperform individual memory and informal communication.

actions.title: Design cognitive artefacts into workflows
actions.description: Build structured checklists, templates, and summaries directly into task flows rather than leaving users to create them informally.

actions.title: Make shared representations available at the point of use
actions.description: Surface the shared state of a collaborative task to all participants without requiring them to request it.

actions.title: Design for the team's cognitive system, not just individual users
actions.description: Consider how the interface connects individual actions to shared understanding and decision-making.

antiPatterns: Collaborative workflows that rely on informal communication rather than structured shared artefacts
Individual-facing interfaces for tasks that are inherently team-distributed
Handover flows with no structured template for context transfer
uiPatterns: Structured handover template with required context fields
Shared status dashboard visible to all participants in real time
Built-in checklist artefact for complex multi-step procedures
examples: Surgical safety checklist integrated into the theatre management system as a required pre-procedure step.
Project handover form with structured fields for current status, blockers, next steps, and key contacts.
principles.designPrompt: What cognitive work can your system absorb so users don't have to hold it in working memory?

principles.name: Situated Cognition
principles.summary: Cognition is inseparable from the context in which it occurs — learning and doing are most effective in situ.
principles.description: Knowledge and skills are best acquired and applied in the context where they will be used. Onboarding and training that is detached from the real work context fails to transfer — guidance embedded at the moment of actual task performance is retained and used far more effectively.
principles.whenToUse: Use in onboarding design, contextual help, and any training or guidance experience that is currently separated from the real workflow.
principles.whyItMatches: This is the theoretical basis for contextual in-app guidance — knowledge acquired in the abstract rarely transfers to the actual task context.

actions.title: Embed guidance at the point of real task execution
actions.description: Surface help, tips, and instructions within the actual task interface, not in a separate training mode.

actions.title: Use real data in training and onboarding
actions.description: Where possible, use the user's own real data or realistic examples in onboarding flows rather than dummy content.

actions.title: Design first-use flows as real task completion, not tours
actions.description: Have new users complete an actual valuable task in onboarding rather than watch a feature demonstration.

antiPatterns: Separate training mode with dummy data that bears no resemblance to real work
Feature tours that walk through empty interfaces without real data
Help documentation that must be read outside the interface before performing the task
uiPatterns: In-context tooltip guidance visible during actual task execution
Onboarding that completes a real first task as the tutorial
Real data preview in setup wizards
examples: Onboarding that guides the user through creating their first real report rather than showing a demo of a completed report.
Contextual tooltip that appears when a user first encounters a complex field, explaining it in the context of their real data.
principles.designPrompt: Observe users in their actual context before designing. Mental models are physically situated.

principles.name: Activity Theory
principles.summary: Human activity is structured hierarchically: objectives, actions to achieve them, and automatic operations.
principles.description: Activity theory distinguishes three levels: the motive-driven objective (why), the goal-directed action (what), and the conditions-driven operation (how). Interfaces that mismatch their design level to the user's current cognitive level create friction — asking users to consciously specify operations they want to automate, or hiding the goal they are trying to achieve.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing complex multi-step workflows, automation features, and any system where the relationship between user goals and interface actions needs alignment.
principles.whyItMatches: Activity theory explains why expert users find wizards patronising (they want to control actions, not be guided through operations) while novices find direct manipulation interfaces intimidating.

actions.title: Align interface level to user expertise level
actions.description: Provide guided, step-by-step flows for novices; direct, efficient action interfaces for experts.

actions.title: Make the goal visible throughout the task
actions.description: Ensure users can always see what objective they are working toward, not just the immediate step.

actions.title: Automate operations that have been mastered
actions.description: Let repeated, mastered operations become automated (keyboard shortcuts, saved settings, smart defaults).

antiPatterns: Expert-level workflows forced into wizard-style step-by-step flows with no bypass option
Interfaces that present low-level operations without showing the higher-level goal
No automation path for operations users perform repeatedly in the same way
uiPatterns: Expert mode bypass for step-by-step wizards
Goal summary visible throughout multi-step task
Saved configurations and templates for repeated operation sequences
examples: Data import tool that offers both a guided 5-step wizard and an advanced direct mapping interface for experienced users.
Approval workflow that shows the final approval objective at the top of every step in the process.
principles.designPrompt: Map the full social context of your task: who else is affected? What rules apply?

principles.name: Proxemics
principles.summary: Spatial distance communicates relationship and importance — UI spacing follows the same cognitive rules.
principles.description: Hall's proxemics theory describes how distance communicates relationship (intimate, personal, social, public). The same principle applies to UI layouts: elements placed in close proximity imply intimate relationship (same group), while distant elements imply separation. Designers control relationship meaning through spatial decisions.
principles.whenToUse: Use when making spacing decisions in dense layouts, card designs, and any information architecture where spatial relationship communicates meaning.
principles.whyItMatches: Proxemics is the anthropological grounding for the gestalt Law of Proximity — both explain why spacing communicates relationship.

actions.title: Use intimate spacing for tightly related elements
actions.description: Labels, inputs, and their associated hints belong within 4-8px of each other — intimate space.

actions.title: Use personal spacing for grouped sections
actions.description: Related sections within a form should be 16-24px apart — personal space.

actions.title: Use social spacing to separate major information blocks
actions.description: Distinct functional areas — header, content, actions — should be 32-48px apart to signal public separation.

antiPatterns: Uniform spacing between all elements regardless of relationship
Dense layouts with no spatial signals of grouping or separation
Large spacing between an input and its directly related label
uiPatterns: 3-tier spacing system: tight (4-8px), medium (16-24px), large (32-48px)
Form layout where label-to-field spacing is tighter than field-to-next-section
Card internal spacing vs card-to-card spacing following proxemic distance rules
examples: Form design using 6px between label and input, 20px between fields, and 40px between form sections.
Dashboard card with 12px internal padding and 24px gap between cards, communicating section membership clearly.
principles.designPrompt: Permission requests should come after users experience benefit. Never on the first screen.

principles.name: Phenomenology
principles.summary: Design should be grounded in the first-person lived experience of users, not system abstractions.
principles.description: Phenomenology insists that the meaning of an experience is constituted by the person living it — not by external observers or system designers. Design grounded in genuine first-person user experience (through observation, diary studies, and contextual enquiry) produces fundamentally different solutions than design grounded in task analysis alone.
principles.whenToUse: Use when framing user research methods, evaluating personas, and any design process where genuine empathy with lived experience is required.
principles.whyItMatches: Most UX design failures stem from designers substituting their own imagined experience for the user's actual lived experience — phenomenology is the corrective.

actions.title: Use diary studies for experience-based insights
actions.description: Ask users to record their experience in-the-moment rather than relying on retrospective recall.

actions.title: Conduct contextual enquiry in actual use environments
actions.description: Observe users in their real work setting, not a lab — context shapes experience.

actions.title: Frame design questions from the user's first-person perspective
actions.description: Ask 'What does it feel like to...' rather than 'What does the user do when...'

antiPatterns: Personas built from demographic data without first-person experiential research
Usability testing in lab conditions that remove the natural work context
Design decisions based on designer empathy-imagination rather than user observation
uiPatterns: Contextual enquiry findings driving interface requirements
Diary study insights surfacing invisible friction points
Experience-based personas grounded in lived context
examples: Intensive care dashboard redesign grounded in 40 hours of contextual observation, revealing that the critical friction was not feature gaps but spatial arrangement during crisis moments.
Onboarding redesigned after diary study revealed users experienced the most anxiety not at complexity but at moments of unexpected silence — no feedback, no confirmation.
principles.designPrompt: Name the primary intentional object on each screen. If you can't name it, the screen has a problem.

principles.name: Pragmatism
principles.summary: Design decisions should be evaluated by their real-world consequences, not theoretical correctness.
principles.description: Pragmatism judges the value of a design decision by whether it produces the desired outcome in practice — not by whether it conforms to a principle in theory. A design that is theoretically elegant but produces worse user outcomes is simply worse. This corrects against dogmatic principle-following without empirical validation.
principles.whenToUse: Use when evaluating competing design decisions, arbitrating between principles, and deciding whether to follow a guideline that may not apply in the current context.
principles.whyItMatches: Pragmatism is the philosophical grounding for user testing over design debates — consequences in practice are the final arbiter of design quality.

actions.title: Test design decisions empirically
actions.description: Do not argue from principle alone — measure the outcome of design decisions with real users.

actions.title: Arbitrate principle conflicts with outcomes data
actions.description: When two principles conflict, determine which produces better real-world outcomes in this specific context.

actions.title: Treat guidelines as hypotheses, not laws
actions.description: Every design principle is a well-evidenced hypothesis — it should be tested, not treated as universally applicable.

antiPatterns: Applying a design principle without validating its relevance to the current context
Resolving design debates through authority or elegance rather than outcome data
Treating pattern libraries as rules that cannot be violated regardless of user evidence
uiPatterns: A/B test before committing to a significant design change
Principle application with hypothesis and measurement plan
Design decision log showing which principles were applied and what outcomes were observed
examples: Reducing form field count based on simplification principles, then testing whether completion rates actually improved before rolling out widely.
Treating the mobile-first design guideline as a hypothesis and testing whether it improves outcomes for the product's actual device distribution.
principles.designPrompt: Test every feature for pragmatic value: does its existence change what users do? If not, remove it.

principles.name: Affordance Theory
principles.summary: Interactive elements must visually signal their own interactivity and the action they afford.
principles.description: An affordance is an action possibility — a button affords clicking, a handle affords pulling. In digital interfaces, affordances must be communicated through signifiers (visual cues) since there is no physical feedback. Elements that look interactive but are not, or that look static but are interactive, create errors and frustration.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing interactive elements, evaluating discoverability, and reviewing any interface where users fail to find or understand controls.
principles.whyItMatches: Most 'where is the button?' usability failures are affordance failures — the element exists but its interactivity is not communicated.

actions.title: Ensure interactive elements are visually distinct from static ones
actions.description: Buttons, links, and controls must look different from non-interactive elements — use colour, border, shadow, or underline.

actions.title: Design hover and focus states for all interactive elements
actions.description: Interactive elements must change appearance on hover and focus to confirm their interactivity.

actions.title: Eliminate false affordances
actions.description: Remove or restyle elements that look interactive but are not — underlined non-link text, button-like decorative elements.

antiPatterns: Flat buttons with no visual differentiation from surrounding text
Clickable text without underline or colour distinction
Decorative borders that look like interactive card elements
uiPatterns: Button with filled background and clear text contrast
Interactive text links with underline or distinct colour
Hover state that changes cursor, colour, or elevation to confirm interactivity
examples: CTA button redesigned from borderless text to filled M3 button — task completion rate increased by 23%.
Clickable table rows given a hover background state to signal interactivity that was previously invisible.
principles.designPrompt: Test every interactive element: is its affordance immediately perceivable without instruction?

principles.name: Chunking
principles.summary: Grouping information into meaningful chunks reduces working memory load and improves recall.
principles.description: Working memory holds approximately 4±1 chunks of information — but a chunk can contain multiple sub-items if they form a meaningful unit (a familiar pattern, a word, a group). Formatting phone numbers, card numbers, and long codes as chunks, and grouping form fields into logical sections, directly reduces working memory cost.
principles.whenToUse: Use whenever presenting long numbers, multi-field forms, complex instructions, or dense information that must be held in working memory.
principles.whyItMatches: Chunking is the most direct application of Miller's Law to practical interface design — segmentation is almost always free to implement and immediately effective.

actions.title: Format long numbers as chunks
actions.description: Display card numbers, ID codes, phone numbers, and IBANs in the conventional chunked format: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

actions.title: Group form fields into semantic sections
actions.description: Visually group related form fields with labels and spacing — treat each section as a chunk.

actions.title: Break long instructional content into numbered steps
actions.description: Convert paragraph instructions into numbered lists of 3-7 steps to support chunked sequential processing.

antiPatterns: Long numeric codes displayed as continuous strings with no chunking
Form fields presented as an undivided list of 20+ items
Complex procedural instructions written as continuous prose
uiPatterns: Auto-formatted input that chunks numbers on entry (card number, phone)
Form sections with group labels and visual spacing
Numbered step list for procedural instructions
examples: Bank card input field that auto-spaces into 4-digit chunks as the user types, reducing transcription errors by 40%.
25-field user profile form reorganised into 4 chunked sections (Personal, Contact, Professional, Preferences), reducing perceived complexity.
principles.designPrompt: Never present raw lists. Always group into meaningful categories of 3–5 items.

principles.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
principles.summary: People continue investing in a failing course of action because of prior investment, not future value.
principles.description: Users who have invested significant time or effort in a partially completed process are more likely to continue even when it is no longer in their interest — the sunk cost fallacy. This can be harnessed ethically to reduce abandonment of genuinely valuable processes, or misused to keep users trapped in harmful or low-value experiences.
principles.whenToUse: Use when designing multi-step processes where partial completion affects willingness to continue, and when reviewing whether progress mechanics are being used ethically.
principles.whyItMatches: Sunk cost explains both why progress bars reduce form abandonment (ethical use) and why platforms deliberately make accounts hard to delete after investment (unethical use).

actions.title: Show invested progress to reduce abandonment of valuable processes
